Dies ist eine Station im Rahmen des Rechtsreferendariats mit einer Mindestdauer von 6 Monaten, idealerweise mit Start im September 2026. Die Stelle ist in Berlin angesiedelt, im hybriden Arbeitsmodell. Deine Aufgaben: Unterstützung bei geschäftskritischen Vertragsangelegenheiten: Prüfung und Koordination des Vertragsabschlusses (z. B. NDAs, SaaS-Verträge, Lieferantenverträge, Mietverträge), unter Sicherstellung der Genauigkeit und Identifizierung zentraler Risiken Unterstützung bei der Pflege und Organisation von Vertragsdatenbanken und -vorlagen Unterstützung beim Management wichtiger regulatorischer und Compliance-Themen: Durchführung rechtlicher und regulatorischer Recherchen in für Via relevanten Bereichen, u. a. Transportnetzwerkdienste, Gig Economy, Versicherungen, Open-Source-Daten und Datenschutzrecht Überwachung der Einhaltung der DSGVO und anderer Datenschutzgesetze durch die Kontrolle von Auftragsverarbeitungsverträgen (DPAs) mit Lieferanten und Partnern Unterstützung der internen Compliance und Corporate Governance von Via Vorantreiben von Effizienz- und Prozessverbesserungen: Aufbau von Kenntnissen interner Datenbanken und Systeme, um aus Daten Erkenntnisse für Geschäftsentscheidungen zu gewinnen Entwicklung und Umsetzung von Maßnahmen zur Effizienzsteigerung des Rechtsteams durch Ticketing-Systeme, Dokumentenmanagement- und Ablagesysteme sowie KPI-Tracking Führende Unterstützung bei der kontinuierlichen Pflege und Verbesserung von Formularen, Prozessen und Systemen Unterstützung bei der Weiterentwicklung rechtlicher Prozesse zur Steigerung von Skalierbarkeit und Effizienz Administrative Unterstützung sowie Mitarbeit an Sonderprojekten nach Bedarf Dein Profil: Du befindest dich aktuell im Rechtsreferendariat und bist berechtigt, eine Station bei einer internen Rechtsabteilung zu absolvieren Erste Erfahrung mit oder Interesse an Tech-, Datenschutz- oder Regulierungsrecht; Kenntnisse der DSGVO von Vorteil Sicherer Umgang mit internen Systemen und Daten - du kannst aus Datenbanken Erkenntnisse für Geschäftsentscheidungen ableiten Klare und präzise Kommunikation, schriftlich wie mündlich, mit der Fähigkeit, komplexe rechtliche Konzepte für fachfremde Stakeholder verständlich zu machen Organisiert und detailorientiert, mit der Fähigkeit, mehrere Arbeitsstränge gleichzeitig zu managen Proaktiv und lernbereit - du übernimmst Eigeninitiative und schöpfst Energie aus der Vielseitigkeit einer internen Rechtsrolle in einem schnell wachsenden Unternehmen Fließend in Englisch und Deutsch; weitere Sprachkenntnisse von Vorteil Was wir bieten: Eine Rolle mit echtem Impact: Via's Technologie bewegt täglich Millionen von Menschen weltweit - und du sorgst dafür, dass das Team dahinter reibungslos funktioniert. Gehalt: 20 € pro Stunde Hybrides Arbeiten in einem schönen Büro im Herzen Berlins an der Chausseestraße, wöchentliche Team-Lunches und gemeinsames Frühstück -und ein Team, das du kennenlernen solltest Urban Sports Club-Mitgliedschaft Bei Via entwickeln wir Technologien, die die Mobilität auf der ganzen Welt zum Besseren verändern. Unser Fokus liegt auf dem Bereich Transit-Tech, denn wir sind überzeugt, dass die Zukunft des Transports in der geteilten, dynamischen und öffentlichen Mobilität liegt. Unser Ansatz reduziert Kohlenstoffemissionen in überlasteten Städten, verringert die Abhängigkeit von privaten Autos und ermöglicht allen Menschen den Zugang zu effizienten und erschwinglichen Möglichkeiten der Fortbewegung. Bereit für die Fahrt? Wir wertschätzen Vielfalt und begrüßen alle Bewerbungen unabhängig von Geschlecht, Nationalität, ethnischer und sozialer Herkunft, Religion/Weltanschauung, Behinderung, Alter sowie sexueller Orientierung und Identität #LI-RB1  #LI-Hybrid #LI-RB1

title: Software Engineer III, Product Safety & Integrity
description: Organisation: Wikimedia Foundation. Location: Remote. Department: Product & Technology. Summary The Wikimedia Foundation is looking for a software engineer to join the Product Safety and Integrity Team . Engineers at the Wikimedia Foundation get to work on technology that truly makes a global impact — powering Wikipedia and its sister projects, which serve billions of pageviews every month across hundreds of languages. It is a rare opportunity to contribute to one of the largest knowledge-sharing platforms in the world, and to help protect free access to information for everyone, everywhere. In this role, you will work in a mostly-remote environment. To ensure there are enough opportunities to communicate, the preferred timezone for this candidate will be UTC - UTC+3. As a software engineer, you will work closely with the team to: Proactively develop and maintain tools that empower communities to identify, mitigate, and prevent various forms of abuse across Wikimedia projects. Design privacy-conscious systems that detect behavioral patterns indicative of abuse while minimizing false positives and respecting user anonymity. Continuously adapt abuse detection and mitigation strategies in response to changes in browser privacy standards, networking protocols, and platform architecture. Collaborate cross-functionally with product managers, designers, and researchers to create holistic, human-centered solutions that balance safety and freedom. Write resilient, maintainable systems and high-quality code with a focus on long-term sustainability. Implement observability to maintain high levels of quality and system stability. Instrument and measure the impact of anti-abuse across Wikimedia projects. Skills and experience: 1+ years related professional experience Experience building and maintaining large-scale applications Proficiency in PHP, Javascript or similar Proficiency in relational databases Strong foundation in security principles Experience in driving cross-team objectives Experience in driving user and product impact Qualities that are important to us: Collaboration, humility, and a shared commitment to Wikimedia’s vision of free knowledge for all which guides everything we build Communicate with clarity and empathy, both in synchronous and asynchronous settings Additionally, we'd love it if you have: Familiarity with abuse fighting or security concerns A history of open source contributions About the Wikimedia Foundation The Wikimedia Foundation is the nonprofit organization that operates Wikipedia and the other Wikimedia free knowledge projects. Our vision is a world in which every single human can freely share in the sum of all knowledge. We believe that everyone has the potential to contribute something to our shared knowledge, and that everyone should be able to access that knowledge freely. We host Wikipedia and the Wikimedia projects, build software experiences for reading, contributing, and sharing Wikimedia content, support the volunteer communities and partners who make Wikimedia possible, and advocate for policies that enable Wikimedia and free knowledge to thrive. The Wikimedia Foundation is a charitable, not-for-profit organization that relies on donations. The Wikimedia Foundation is a United States 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organization with offices in San Francisco, California, USA. title: Frontier Agents Engineer (Forward Deployed Engineering)
description: Organisation: Scale AI. Location: San Francisco, CA; New York, NY. Department: Enterprise Engineering. Office: New York, NY, San Francisco, CA. About Scale AI Scale AI is the data foundation for AI, helping organizations build and deploy reliable production AI applications. We partner with the world's leading enterprises and government organizations to accelerate their AI transformation through frontier AI systems that solve real business problems. Every day, we work with organizations across finance, healthcare, manufacturing, media, telecommunications, and government to build production AI agents that automate complex workflows, reason over enterprise knowledge, and operate safely at scale. The Opportunity The hardest part of enterprise AI isn't building a great model—it's building AI systems that reliably operate inside complex production environments. As a Frontier Agent Engineer (Forward Deployed Engineering) , you'll work directly with strategic enterprise customers to architect, integrate, deploy, and operate production AI systems. You'll combine modern software engineering, distributed systems, cloud infrastructure, and frontier AI technologies to transform cutting-edge models into reliable enterprise software. Unlike traditional infrastructure or platform roles, you'll work at the intersection of AI and enterprise engineering. You'll design production agent architectures, integrate with customer systems, deploy AI into mission-critical workflows, and help shape the engineering best practices for the next generation of enterprise AI. If you enjoy solving difficult systems problems, rapidly prototyping new AI capabilities, and bringing frontier AI into production, you'll fit right in. What You'll Build Enterprise AI Systems Architect and deploy production AI systems that integrate seamlessly into complex enterprise environments, including cloud platforms, data warehouses, internal APIs, business applications, and proprietary software systems. Design scalable agent architectures that combine LLMs, retrieval, memory, tools, structured knowledge, and enterprise data into reliable production workflows. Build robust integrations that allow AI agents to safely interact with customer systems while meeting enterprise requirements for security, governance, and compliance. Rapidly prototype new AI capabilities and evolve successful prototypes into production-ready systems. AI Platform Engineering Build the production infrastructure that enables frontier AI research to become reliable enterprise software. Develop agent runtimes, orchestration frameworks, context pipelines, execution services, and tool integrations that power production AI systems. Engineer systems for reliability, observability, latency, scalability, retries, fallback strategies, and graceful degradation. Design human-in-the-loop workflows that effectively combine AI automation with expert oversight. Build deployment patterns that allow AI systems to evolve safely through continuous delivery and experimentation. Production AI Quality Operationalize modern AI quality systems that ensure production agents remain reliable as models, prompts, and customer data evolve. Deploy evaluation harnesses using offline benchmarks, online experiments, golden datasets, regression suites, and LLM-as-a-Judge to detect quality regressions before they impact customers. Implement tracing, observability, monitoring, guardrails, grounding, and safety mechanisms that enable production AI systems to operate with confidence. Partner closely with Applied AI engineers to productionize new evaluation methodologies, retrieval strategies, reasoning architectures, and emerging AI capabilities. Rapidly evaluate newly released models, agent frameworks, evaluation methodologies, and developer tooling, determining how they can be safely adopted into production systems. Customer Innovation Partner directly with enterprise customers to understand their technical infrastructure, software architecture, and operational workflows. Translate ambiguous customer problems into scalable production AI architectures. Collaborate with customer software engineers, ML engineers, platform teams, and product organizations to deploy AI into mission-critical workflows. Identify reusable engineering patterns that become core capabilities across multiple enterprise deployments. Technical Leadership Serve as the primary technical advisor for strategic enterprise accounts. Lead architecture discussions spanning distributed systems, AI infrastructure, enterprise integration, and production deployment. Document reusable architecture patterns, deployment strategies, integration frameworks, and operational best practices. Work closely with Scale's product, infrastructure, and Applied AI teams to continuously improve the platform. What Makes This Role Different You'll work across the full lifecycle of production AI systems: Architecting enterprise AI systems and agent platforms Building integrations across cloud infrastructure and enterprise software Deploying AI agents into production environments Operationalizing evaluation frameworks, guardrails, and observability Running production experiments and measuring real-world business impact Continuously improving deployed AI systems using customer feedback and operational telemetry You'll work with the latest frontier AI models, evaluation methodologies, agent frameworks, and developer tooling as they emerge, helping customers adopt new AI capabilities safely and effectively. Rather than supporting a single product or platform, you'll solve diverse engineering challenges across industries and use cases, rapidly building expertise across enterprise architecture, AI systems engineering, and production deployment. Required Qualifications 4+ years of software engineering experience with strong fundamentals in distributed systems, data structures, algorithms, and system design. Strong Python programming skills with experience building production software. Experience building or deploying AI-powered applications using modern LLM APIs, agent frameworks, MCP, retrieval systems, or vector databases. Experience with cloud platforms (AWS, Azure, or GCP) and modern production infrastructure. Strong problem-solving skills with the ability to navigate ambiguous technical requirements and rapidly iterate toward production solutions. Excellent communication skills and the ability to work directly with enterprise engineering teams. title: Staff Software Engineer, RL Environments
description: Organisation: Scale AI. Location: San Francisco, CA; New York, NY. Department: Gen AI Engineering. Office: San Francisco, CA. About Scale AI At Scale, our mission is to develop reliable AI systems for the world's most important decisions. Our products provide the high-quality data and full-stack technologies that power the world's leading models, and help enterprises and governments build, deploy, and oversee AI applications that deliver real impact. Scale Frontier Data is the organization behind the training and evaluation data that frontier labs depend on. We build the systems, tooling, and expert workflows that turn hard human expertise into signals that models can learn from, across reasoning, coding, agentic tool use, and domain expertise. Reinforcement learning environments are now the center of gravity for that work: the difference between a model that demos well and a model that reliably completes long-horizon work is almost always the quality of the environments and reward signals it was trained against. Responsibilities As a Staff Software Engineer, RL Environments, you'll own the technical foundation for how Scale builds, runs, verifies, and delivers RL environments at scale. An RL environment is a real piece of software: a containerized world with real dependencies, real state, real tools, and a grader that has to be correct even when the agent is creative about breaking it. Building one is a full-stack engineering problem. Building thousands of them reproducibly, cheaply, with trustworthy reward signals and throughput measured in millions of rollouts is a systems problem that very few people have solved. You'll work on both. You'll design the platform: sandboxed execution, environment packaging and versioning, rollout orchestration, trajectory capture, verifier frameworks, and the authoring surfaces that let engineers and domain experts produce environments without reinventing infrastructure each time. And you'll go deep on the environments themselves by instrumenting real applications, designing task suites that expose specific capability gaps, and building graders that hold up under adversarial optimization. This is a hands-on engineering role. You'll set technical direction across multiple teams, and you'll still be the person who writes the hard part. Required Qualifications 8+ years of software engineering experience with strong fundamentals in distributed systems, system design, data structures, and algorithms. title: Tooling: add a deterministic CPU semantic simulator and virtual GPU runtime
description:
Open-source contribution opportunity. Repository: harsh-nod/fe2o3. Labels: enhancement, help wanted, priority:P2, area:tooling. ## Objective

Allow developers and CI to compile, verify, execute, inspect, and debug admitted
fe2o3 kernels when no physical GPU is available.

The primary deliverable is a deterministic CPU **semantic simulator** for
canonical fe2o3 KIR plus a bounded virtual runtime. It is not an AMDGPU ISA
emulator and not a GPU performance model.

The simulator should answer:

- Does this admitted kernel produce the expected outputs for these exact inputs
  and launch dimensions?
- What does each work-item, lane, wave, and workgroup do?
- Which memory access, barrier, atomic, or collective first violates its
  contract?
- Does the host-side operation graph respect allocation, dependency, queue,
  completion, and collective lifetimes?
- Can a failure be reproduced, reduced, visualized, and queried without GPU
  access?
- Which results remain unvalidated until physical hardware executes the exact
  artifact?

Simulation must be explicit. fe2o3 must never silently run on CPU after a GPU
launch was requested, and simulated success must never count as hardware,
AMDGPU ISA, driver, runtime, performance, or parity evidence.

## Scope boundary

This issue covers:

- functional execution of canonical verified KIR;
- deterministic and seeded work-item/wave/workgroup scheduling;
- target-profile semantic models for admitted GPU operations;
- memory, initialization, bounds, alias, race, atomic, barrier, and collective
  diagnostics;
- a virtual device/runtime for allocations, copies, queues, dispatches,
  signals, dependencies, failures, and optional multi-device functional tests;
- structured execution traces and integration with #215;
- headless and agent-native APIs; and
- differential qualification against physical GPU execution when hardware is
  available.

This issue explicitly excludes:

- cycle-accurate or timing-accurate simulation;
- predicting runtime, throughput, bandwidth, occupancy, cache behavior,
  instruction scheduling, or communication/computation overlap;
- treating CPU wall-clock time as evidence about GPU performance;
- executing HSACO or emulating the complete AMDGPU ISA;
- reproducing undocumented driver, firmware, cache, or weak-memory behavior;
  and
- transparent production fallback from a requested GPU to CPU.

Static compiler resource accounting may still run without a GPU, but it is not
CPU performance prediction and remains owned by compiler/profiler work.

## Current baseline

fe2o3 has useful independent models and oracles, but no general CPU kernel
simulator:

- 'fe2o3-differential' evaluates a bounded independent-work-item scalar
  expression subset with deterministic wrapping-'i32' CPU semantics.
- Its semantic conformance corpus models bounded pointer distance, volatile
  memory, non-overlapping copies, Rust layouts, integer switches, atomic
  operations, bounds, and cross-lane race obligations.
- Existing hardware tests compare exact kernels with independent CPU oracles
  and canaries.
- Committed target-specific golden records, such as gfx942 FP8/FNUZ behavior,
  can be consumed in generic CI without a GPU.
- KIR is target-neutral, versioned, typed SSA with explicit address spaces,
  memory effects, launch queries, barriers, atomics, workgroup memory, wave
  width, capabilities, and deterministic verification.
- 'fe2o3-kernel-analysis' already produces bounded per-invocation memory and
  barrier traces for a closed static Pliron subset.
- 'fe2o3-runtime-model' is a bounded, syscall-free executable state machine for
  device, VM, allocation, mapping, code, queue, dispatch, and completion
  lifecycles.

These pieces are test or proof-support infrastructure. They do not currently
execute an arbitrary admitted KIR module, simulate wave/workgroup behavior, or
provide a virtual host runtime through the normal fe2o3 interface.

The architecture also requires one real kernel algorithm body. A simulator
must interpret the canonical semantic representation derived from that body;
it must not generate or maintain a second algorithm-specific CPU
implementation. Independent CPU oracles remain valuable comparison references,
not the kernel implementation.

## Why fe2o3 can be different

A general HIP CPU runtime can map HIP source constructs onto CPU threads, and
Triton already has a useful CPU interpreter. Merely adding a sequential KIR
interpreter is therefore not enough.

fe2o3 can differentiate through one integrated semantic contract:

- the simulator executes the same canonical KIR consumed by target lowering;
- every step retains stable source, MIR, KIR, schedule, property, and artifact
  identities;
- typed regions preserve allocation identity, bounds, alignment, address
  space, mutability, alias, and initialization state;
- wave width, active masks, collectives, barriers, LDS epochs, atomics, and
  memory scope are explicit rather than reconstructed from C++ macros;
- proof/property records can be displayed beside dynamic simulation evidence
  without conflating proof and observation;
- deterministic schedule exploration can reproduce synchronization and race
  failures and produce minimal semantic traces;
- the existing virtual runtime model can exercise queue/resource/completion and
  distributed-graph correctness without inventing fake hardware handles; and
- the same trace/query schema can drive humans, CI, reducers, and agents.

The quality bar is semantic fidelity and diagnosis, not CPU execution speed.

## Simulation contract

### 1. What is executed

Interpret only a canonical, decoded, and successfully verified KIR module plus:

- exact kernel/algorithm identity;
- typed launch descriptor and dimensions;
- explicit simulated target profile;
- canonical argument and memory-object snapshots;
- admitted operation and capability registry;
- numerical and memory-model policy;
- scheduler policy and seed;
- resource and step bounds; and
- optional property/proof records for correlation.

Do not interpret source text, displayed names, arbitrary LLVM IR, or HSACO.
Do not bypass KIR verification. Unknown operations, capabilities, contracts, or
versions fail with structured 'Unsupported' results.

The simulated target profile may select facts such as wave32 versus wave64,
supported operation families, address-space rules, numerical contracts, and
workgroup limits. Selecting 'gfx942' means "use the admitted gfx942 semantic
profile"; it does not claim that gfx942 hardware executed the kernel.

### 2. Execution hierarchy

Represent the hierarchy explicitly:

~~~text
grid
  -> workgroup
    -> wave
      -> lane / logical work-item
        -> SSA values, control state, and memory effects
~~~

Required semantics include:

- 1D/2D/3D grid and local coordinates;
- partial final waves and active masks;
- per-work-item private state;
- per-workgroup LDS and barrier state;
- shared grid/global and constant memory;
- divergent control flow and reconvergence at the semantic IR level;
- exact wave32/wave64 collective participation;
- workgroup barriers and fences;
- scoped atomics and modeled happens-before edges; and
- explicit completion, trap, assertion, and unsupported-operation states.

Grid workgroups may be executed independently when semantics permit. Their CPU
execution order must not become a guarantee about hardware order.

### 3. Deterministic schedulers

Provide at least:

- **canonical**: a stable default order for reproducible tests and debugging;
- **seeded**: a reproducible alternate legal schedule;
- **replay**: re-execute an exact previously recorded simulator schedule; and
- **bounded exploration**: enumerate or systematically perturb legal
  interleavings for small synchronization/race cases.

A passing single schedule is functional evidence for that simulated execution,
not proof of race freedom. Bounded exploration reports its exact state/schedule
coverage and cannot claim absence outside that bound.

Record scheduling decisions by semantic workgroup/wave/lane identity, never by
CPU thread ID. A correct first implementation may be single-threaded. Host
parallelism is an optimization only after deterministic behavior is preserved.

### 4. Memory model

Use a typed virtual address space, not raw host pointers. Every pointer/value
must retain:

- allocation and generation identity;
- address space;
- byte offset and extent;
- alignment;
- readable/writable/atomic permissions;
- initialization state;
- provenance and alias/ownership relation; and
- lifetime state.

Detect and report:

- out-of-bounds and misaligned accesses;
- uninitialized reads;
- use after release or stale generation;
- illegal address-space access;
- forbidden alias or concurrent non-atomic access;
- overlapping 'copy_nonoverlapping';
- unsupported atomic scope/order/width; and
- workgroup-memory epoch and lifetime errors.

Poison/uninitialized state must propagate through typed values without invoking
host undefined behavior. The simulator itself should contain no unsafe host
memory access for device loads/stores.

### 5. Synchronization, waves, and collectives

Wave operations execute over an explicit active mask and wave width.
Workgroup barriers require every required live participant to reach a compatible
barrier phase. Report divergent exit, mismatched barrier, deadlock, and
out-of-order LDS epoch with the participating semantic identities.

Implement collectives from admitted semantic contracts. Never replace a wave
or workgroup collective with an ordinary scalar fold unless the implementation
preserves its participation, mask, ordering, and numerical contract.

Atomic and fence simulation must use an explicit versioned model. Deterministic
serialization can be one execution strategy but cannot be presented as proof
that a racy program is valid.

### 6. Numerical semantics

Integer widths, overflow, shifts, casts, comparisons, and poison behavior must
be explicit and independent of the host compiler.

For floating point:

- use exact bit-level or reviewed software semantics where available;
- bind rounding, denormal, NaN, signed-zero, fast-math, reduction-order, and
  contraction policy to the operation/target profile;
- use committed hardware-derived golden tables only for their stated domain;
- model matrix/MFMA operations only after their numerical contract is
  implemented; and
- return 'UnsupportedNumericalContract' instead of approximating an unmodeled
  target operation with host arithmetic.

A simulator result may be target-profile semantic evidence, but it is not
machine-refinement evidence for LLVM/ISA or physical hardware.

### 7. External and unsafe operations

Inline assembly, external device libraries, opaque intrinsics, hostcalls, and
other unsafe/contracted operations require one of:

- a reviewed executable semantic model;
- an explicit bounded user-supplied test double whose identity appears in the
  result; or
- a structured unsupported result.

A proof contract alone is not executable behavior. A test double is not proof
or hardware evidence.

## Virtual runtime

Add an explicit virtual-device backend over 'fe2o3-runtime-model'. It should
exercise host behavior without KFD/HSA/HIP:

- virtual device inventory and target capabilities;
- allocation, mapping, typed copies, and lifetime checks;
- code/KIR admission without pretending to load HSACO;
- queues, dispatch publication, completion, and failures;
- streams/events or direct-KFD dependency equivalents where admitted;
- deterministic dependency DAG execution;
- cancellation, timeout observation, ambiguous publication, reset, and
  quiescence cases; and
- bounded virtual multi-device transfers and collectives after #182 defines
  their canonical plans.

Virtual time is a deterministic ordering/testing mechanism only. It is not a
GPU timing estimate. Functional multi-device simulation may validate shards,
versions, dependencies, collective membership, and failure handling, but not
bandwidth or overlap performance.

The virtual backend grants no KFD, HSA, HIP, device, artifact-load, or dispatch
authority. Its handles and addresses are simulation-local identities.

## Developer interface

Add an explicit command such as:

~~~text
cargo fe2o3 simulate [OPTIONS] --kernel KERNEL -- INPUTS
~~~

Initial options should cover:

~~~text
--target-profile gfx942
--scheduler canonical|seeded|explore
--seed N
--max-steps N
--max-schedules N
--trace PATH
--break SITE
--watch REGION
--virtual-runtime
--format human|json
~~~

Exact spelling can be settled in the CLI ADR. Required behavior:

- 'cargo fe2o3 build', KIR verification, static inspection, and simulation can
  run without enumerating a physical GPU when their other tool dependencies
  are installed.
- Commands that require hardware return a typed 'HardwareUnavailable' result;
  they do not skip successfully or invoke simulation implicitly.
- Output prominently identifies 'simulated=true', simulator version, target
  profile, scheduler/seed, coverage bounds, KIR identity, and absence of
  hardware validation.
- A later physical run can consume the same canonical input snapshot and
  compare output and semantic events through the differential infrastructure.

## Debugger, trace, and agent integration

Integrate with #215's semantic capture schema. The simulator should emit an
event stream containing:

- source/MIR/KIR semantic site;
- workgroup, wave, active mask, and lane/work-item identity;
- SSA definitions and selected typed values;
- branches and reconvergence;
- memory allocation/region, address, width, and access result;
- barrier, fence, atomic, LDS epoch, and collective phase;
- scheduler decision and happens-before relation;
- property/proof references; and
- trap, assertion, deadlock, race, unsupported, and bound-exhaustion results.

Support deterministic stepping by semantic operation, lane, wave, workgroup,
barrier phase, and memory access. Checkpoints plus replay may provide reverse
inspection without promising reverse execution on hardware.

Expose the same bounded read-only operations proposed by #215, including
'inspect_workgroup', 'inspect_wave', 'inspect_lane', 'inspect_memory_access',
'inspect_barrier', and 'inspect_property'. Add:

~~~text
simulate
list_schedules
replay_schedule
explore_interleavings
compare_simulation_to_hardware
reduce_simulation_failure
~~~

Stateful simulation requests must carry explicit input/resource limits.
Structured results must cite exact trace records and distinguish 'declared',
'proved', 'simulated', 'hardware-observed', 'inferred', and 'unavailable'.

## Roadmap

### C0: Semantics and competitive baseline

- Compare official HIP, the archived/incomplete HIP-CPU implementation,
  Triton's interpreter, Mojo CPU/GPU behavior, and relevant Rust GPU tools.
- Define the interpretation boundary, target-profile contract, unsupported
  behavior, scheduler semantics, memory model, numerical policy, and evidence
  taxonomy.
- Decide crate ownership and stable schemas with #134, #175, #215, and #137.
- Publish a no-GPU capability matrix for toolchain-only, ROCm-toolchain, and
  hardware-required workflows.

Exit when each accepted KIR operation is either assigned a precise simulator
semantic owner or explicitly unsupported.

### C1: Scalar KIR interpreter

- Execute verified SSA control flow, calls, integer/scalar operations, launch
  queries, and typed global loads/stores.
- Implement canonical inputs, outputs, errors, resource bounds, and traces.
- Reuse existing 'fe2o3-differential' scalar cases as an independent oracle.
- Add deterministic failure reduction.

Exit when generated scalar cases agree with the independent evaluator and
malformed/unsupported modules fail structurally rather than panicking.

### C2: Typed memory and Rust semantics

- Add aggregates, enums, layouts, casts, pointer provenance, address spaces,
  initialization/poison, copies, volatile access, and region effects.
- Exercise all semantic conformance corpus cases.
- Add source/MIR/KIR trace correlation and hostile stale-identity tests.

Exit when memory failures identify the exact semantic operation, work-item,
allocation/region, contract, and provenance without raw host-pointer behavior.

### C3: Wave and workgroup simulator

- Add wave32/wave64 active masks, divergence/reconvergence, wave collectives,
  LDS, fences, workgroup barriers, atomics, and admitted matrix contracts.
- Implement canonical, seeded, replay, and bounded-exploration schedulers.
- Add race, deadlock, divergent-barrier, collective-mask, and LDS-epoch
  diagnostics.

Exit when Wave64 collective, workgroup synchronization, tiled transpose, and
one admitted LDS GEMM profile execute correctly, and seeded mutations produce
stable minimal traces.

### C4: Virtual host runtime

- Adapt the executable runtime model into an explicitly non-authoritative
  virtual backend.
- Add allocations, mappings, copies, queues, dispatches, dependencies,
  completions, cancellation/failure, and resource-lifetime diagnostics.
- Use the KIR interpreter as the dispatch executor.
- Add functional virtual multi-device data-version and collective plans only
  after #182 defines those semantics.

Exit when normal generated host interfaces can execute a bounded graph against
a virtual device with no GPU libraries or device nodes, while misuse and fault
injection produce the modeled terminal states.

### C5: Debugger and agent workflow

- Emit #215-compatible semantic captures.
- Add workgroup/wave/lane stepping, watches, breakpoints, schedule replay, and
  reverse inspection through deterministic checkpoints.
- Implement bounded query, interleaving exploration, comparison, and reducer
  APIs.
- Add seeded agent diagnosis fixtures.

Exit when a human and an agent can independently diagnose and reduce seeded
memory, barrier, race, and host-lifetime failures without GPU access and with
evidence IDs for every conclusion.

### C6: Differential qualification

- Run each supported semantic family against physical CDNA/RDNA targets when
  hardware is available.
- Bind canonical input, KIR, target profile, simulator, compiler, artifact,
  runtime, and device identities.
- Preserve discrepancies as first-class results and reduce them.
- Maintain committed hardware-derived goldens only through reviewed update
  procedures.
- Report simulator coverage separately from hardware coverage in dashboards.

Exit when supported simulator semantics have committed differential cases,
known mismatches are explicit, and generic no-GPU CI cannot increase hardware
or parity pass counts.

## Initial acceptance cases

1. **No device:** on a host with no '/dev/kfd', HIP/HSA runtime, or GPU, a
   supported scalar kernel compiles to canonical KIR and simulates with exact
   typed output; hardware execution returns 'HardwareUnavailable'.
2. **Per-lane memory fault:** one seeded work-item accesses outside its typed
   region and the result identifies source/KIR site, grid/workgroup/wave/lane,
   allocation, offset, legal extent, and property status.
3. **Divergent barrier:** a subset of a workgroup skips a barrier and canonical
   plus explored schedules report the incompatible participants and phase.
4. **Wave collective:** partial-wave and divergent-mask cases preserve exact
   Wave64 participation and reduction/scan order for the admitted contract.
5. **Race exploration:** two legal schedules produce different results; the
   report includes both schedules, conflicting accesses, happens-before state,
   and the bounded coverage statement.
6. **Virtual runtime misuse:** an early release, stale allocation generation,
   or ambiguous completion is rejected by the virtual runtime with the same
   canonical lifecycle state used by the executable model.
7. **Differential replay:** when a GPU is later available, the same input
   snapshot runs on the physical target and produces a structured simulator
   versus hardware comparison.
8. **Unsupported target operation:** inline assembly or an unmodeled MFMA
   numerical contract returns a typed unsupported result and is never replaced
   by approximate host execution.

## Evidence rules

- Simulator execution is labeled **simulated observation**.
- Independent CPU-oracle agreement is labeled **differential model agreement**.
- Verus/property evidence remains **proved** only for its exact statement and
  refinement boundary.
- Physical execution is labeled **hardware observation** with exact device and
  artifact identity.
- Only a separately admitted refinement can relate these layers.
- No simulator result authorizes compilation, publication, load, dispatch, or
  proof admission.
- No simulator result updates a hardware parity row.
- CPU execution duration is never reported as predicted GPU duration.

## Non-goals

- Do not compile the kernel body as an ordinary host Rust function.
- Do not maintain a second algorithm-specific CPU implementation.
- Do not execute unverified KIR.
- Do not silently substitute CPU simulation for a requested GPU.
- Do not use CPU threads as the semantic identity of GPU work-items.
- Do not serialize racy operations and then claim race freedom.
- Do not approximate unsupported target numerical behavior.
- Do not execute HSACO or emulate the full AMDGPU ISA in this issue.
- Do not model GPU timing, performance, caches, occupancy, pipelines, bandwidth,
  or compute/communication overlap.
- Do not treat virtual time or CPU wall-clock measurements as GPU evidence.

## Dependencies and ownership

- #134 and #175/#176-#181 own canonical KIR and production compiler
  convergence. The simulator consumes their verified representation.
- #215 owns the shared semantic capture, visualization, and agent-query model.
  This issue provides simulated events and deterministic replay.
- 'fe2o3-differential' remains the independent generated oracle and reducer
  foundation; it should not become a circular wrapper around the simulator.
- 'fe2o3-kernel-analysis' owns static analysis. Dynamic simulator observations
  can be compared with but do not replace its proof/analysis results.
- #107/#108 and property-specific verification work own proof and
  machine-refinement claims.
- #137 owns the authoritative direct-KFD runtime. The virtual backend consumes
  its executable model but grants no production authority.
- #182 owns async/distributed plans. Functional virtual multi-device support

Stop overpaying for law firm work. Start with Axiom. About the Role: The successful candidate will lead the global accounting, tax, treasury, and financial reporting operations of the Company with overall responsibility for all aspects of the monthly close process. They will be responsible for analyzing financial results and will play a pivotal role in the preparation for & execution of periodic audits, including for our international entities. This role will also be required to routinely interact with the heads of other departments to ensure unknown/un-invoiced expenses are captured timely. Responsibilities: •    Lead the Global Accounting teams (including Revenue/AR, AP and Payroll) and resolves daily team technical accounting queries. •    Oversee all aspects of accounting and ensure the month close is completed accurately per US GAAP and within the monthly close cycle, including the preparation and review of all Balance Sheet account reconciliations and key accruals. •    Prepare and presents monthly financial statements to management and support development and preparation of monthly management accounting package •    Oversee tax and statutory financial statement compliance with applicable international and domestic regulations •    Perform other accounting, financial, or administrative tasks as may be required from time to time, on short notice from Management. •    Oversee treasury and cash management functions, including liquidity planning and cash flow forecasting •    Being owned by Private Equity, assist in the preparation for an upcoming due diligence and be a central figure in this potential due diligence, be involved in the payment of special dividends and assist in potential buying M&A opportunities •    Manage banking relationships and coordinate external debt activities and compliance •    Ensure that company financial records & reports are maintained in compliance with company policies & US GAAP (accrual basis). Responsible for preparing monthly/quarterly draft financial statements, forecasts, account reconciliations & other documents to ensure this compliance. •    Build strong relationships within the accounting and overall finance teams, as well as cross-functionally in order to support the Company’s business needs •    Ensure a strong internal financial control environment across the entire accounting team and help identify & drive continuous process improvements. •    Ensure thoughtful, timely and accurate research and documentation of technical accounting matters •    Ensure only valid expenses with proper management authorization are paid. •    Review balance sheet account schedules & reconciliations. •    Establish solid working relationships with audit, tax, and accounting vendors & service providers and serve as the primary point of coordination with external auditors and tax advisors •    This is a fast-growing dynamic environment & the candidate must have willingness to pitch-in when asked to support other areas. In the first 12 months, the Controller will need to spend time understanding the current organization and processes.  In addition, the successful candidate will focus on the following accountabilities: •    Learn the key aspects of the unique business model and understand performance beyond just the numbers, both in terms of current performance as well as long-term strategic plans. •    Develop relationships across the organization. The successful candidate will need to understand the needs of each function and develop a more client service orientation for the finance organization.  The challenge will be to help install processes and controls without negatively impacting a strong growth culture. •    Review and improve key processes, including the order to cash process for improvements and compliance •    Partner with the IT organization to ensure that the systems of the company meet the needs of today and the future. The annual base salary range for this role located in Chicago, Illinois is $200,000 - $230,000 + 30% bonus depending on experience. You can also participate in our benefits programs that include healthcare, life and disability coverage, 401K with company match, paid sick and personal time off, paid parental leave and more . title: Research Scientist, Safety Post Training
description: Organisation: Scale AI. Location: San Francisco, CA; New York, NY. Department: Research. Office: San Francisco, CA. Scale Labs, Research Scientist — Safety Post Training As the leading data and evaluation partner for frontier AI companies, Scale plays an integral role in understanding the capabilities and safeguarding AI models and systems. Building on this expertise, Scale Labs has launched a new team focused on policy research, to bridge the gap between AI research and global policymakers to make informed, scientific decisions about AI risks and capabilities. Our research tackles the hardest problems in agent robustness, AI control protocols, and AI risk evaluations to help governments, industry, and the public understand and mitigate AI risk while maximizing AI adoption. This team collaborates broadly across industry, the public sector, and academia and regularly publishes our findings. We are actively seeking talented researchers to join us in shaping this vision. As a Research Scientist working on Safety Post-Training you will develop and apply post-training methods and interpretability techniques to make frontier AI systems safer, and better understood by researchers and policymakers.. For example, you might: Design and run post-training pipelines to study how training choices affect model safety, robustness, and alignment properties; Develop interpretability-informed evaluations that reveal how and why models produce unsafe, deceptive, or otherwise undesirable behaviors, and use those insights to guide targeted mitigations; Collaborate with policymakers, engineers, and other researchers to translate post-training and interpretability findings into actionable safety standards, evaluation benchmarks, and best practices. Experience with post-training and RL techniques such as RLHF, DPO, GRPO, and similar approaches. A track record of published research in machine learning, particularly in generative AI. At least three years of experience addressing sophisticated ML problems, whether in a research setting or in product development. Strong written and verbal communication skills to operate in a cross-functional team. title: Fundraising Support Specialist (Contract)
description: Organisation: Wikimedia Foundation. Location: Remote. Department: Advancement. Summary The Wikimedia Foundation seeks a Fundraising Support Specialist to join our Online Fundraising team, reporting to the Senior Manager of Fundraising Products. In this role, you will perform vital production tasks to enable our team of Revenue Specialists to launch and optimize fundraising campaigns in more than 20 languages and 30 countries each year. In a typical day, you will: Work in web files to modify HTML and CSS content as part of the production process for our international campaigns, in coordination with Revenue Specialists. This involves finding and updating translation elements, implementing copy tests, and interfacing with linguists and creative strategists to verify test content before it goes live. Work in our CentralNotice banner delivery platform to implement new campaigns and banner tests. Guided by test priorities from the Revenue Specialists, you will ensure test content is ready and organized for clarity of reporting. Manage QA processes for our banner program, which includes cross-browser review and the implementation of a “QA checklist” maintained by our design team. If bugs are found, you will work with developers and designers to triage and verify their solutions. Receive instructions on new tasks from Revenue Specialists and the Senior Manager of Fundraising Products. You will maintain your own Asana board of priorities and contribute to other Asana workflows to ensure campaign delivery. Desired Skills and Qualifications: Familiarity with HTML and CSS; JS is a ‘nice to have’ but optional. This position is not a developer role, but comfort navigating code, implementing test overrides, and verifying your changes is required. Excellent attention to detail, and the ability to own and maintain quality assurance processes. Solid written and verbal communication skills and the ability to perform autonomously in a remote, time-zone distributed environment. A desire to learn on the job and adapt to Wikimedia’s unique movement and model. Experience with multilingual marketing or programs, and comfort working within distributed, international environments. December is a critical fundraising month and team members are generally needed to work in this month. Occasional travel, approximately 2 times a year, including internationally. About the Wikimedia Foundation The Wikimedia Foundation is the nonprofit organization that operates Wikipedia and the other Wikimedia free knowledge projects. Our vision is a world in which every single human can freely share in the sum of all knowledge. We believe that everyone has the potential to contribute something to our shared knowledge, and that everyone should be able to access that knowledge freely. We host Wikipedia and the Wikimedia projects, build software experiences for reading, contributing, and sharing Wikimedia content, support the volunteer communities and partners who make Wikimedia possible, and advocate for policies that enable Wikimedia and free knowledge to thrive. The Wikimedia Foundation is a charitable, not-for-profit organization that relies on donations. We receive donations from millions of individuals around the world, with an average donation of about $15. We also receive donations through institutional grants and gifts. The Wikimedia Foundation is a United States 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organization with offices in San Francisco, California, USA. As an equal opportunity employer, the Wikimedia Foundation values having a diverse workforce and continuously strives to maintain an inclusive and equitable workplace. We encourage people with a diverse range of backgrounds to apply. ### Definition of done

- [ ] For each of the 14 rows above, open the linked Google Form (if accessible) or use the title/content to determine which single canonical chapter (9.1-9.8, per `cert_mapping/README.md`) it actually belongs to.
- [ ] Explicitly confirm whether canonical 9.5 is genuinely uncovered by any existing quiz row, or whether one of the 14 rows is mislabeled 9.5 content.
- [ ] Flag any rows that appear to be duplicate content under different IDs (starting from the "Value Alignment Frameworks" and "Standards and Frameworks for AI Governance" title clusters above), and note which is likely canonical/authoritative and which is likely a stale renumbering.
- [ ] For each row, propose either (a) a corrected canonical chapter ID, or (b) a recommendation to merge/retire it if it duplicates another row's content.
- [ ] Findings posted as comments in this issue thread against the review checklist.
- [ ] Final outcome recorded on this issue: accept / minor revisions / major revisions.
- [ ] If revisions were made, a linked PR implements them and references this issue (keep to ~20 changed items or fewer per PR, per `CONTRIBUTING.md`).

### Estimated effort

Small (~1-3 hours) — bounded to 14 rows in one file, but each row needs a Form check or careful title/content comparison, so budget on the higher end of "small."

### Required skills

Comfortable reading Google Forms and short markdown tables; enough familiarity with the book's Part 9 subject matter (AI safety, governance, and compliance topics — output filtering, alignment, GDPR, AI governance standards) to judge whether a quiz's questions plausibly match a given canonical chapter title.

### Exemplar to follow

This review follows the JOSE-style open review convention described in `_cfc/workstreams.md` §2: conducted as a checklist-driven GitHub issue thread, not a private review. Every finding should carry a **location** (row ID), a **description**, **evidence** (a Form-link comparison, a title/content quote), and a **proposed fix** — see `_cfc/workstreams.md` §2 for the full description of what a finding should look like. See also https://jose.theoj.org/about#reviewer_guidelines for the general review-checklist-as-issue-thread model.

### Additional notes

Questions? Check `SUPPORT.md` before opening a new issue. This issue is part of the quiz/practice-test review sub-track (`_cfc/workstreams.md` §2.3), which found chapter-ID drift in Parts 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, and 10 of `quizzes_ver20JUN26.md` — Part 9 is the single largest mismatch (14 quiz rows against 8 canonical chapters) and is prioritized first for that reason.

title: Staff Network Engineer, App Platform
description: Organisation: Scale AI. Location: San Francisco, CA. Department: Applications Platform Engineering. Office: San Francisco, CA. Scale GP (Scale Generative AI Platform) is Scale’s enterprise AI platform, providing APIs and infrastructure for knowledge retrieval, inference, evaluation, agents, and more. We deploy SGP across AWS, Azure, and GCP, often directly into customer-controlled cloud environments across highly regulated industries including healthcare, financial services, telecom, and retail. As SGP has grown in scale and complexity, networking has become a critical architectural discipline of its own. Today, teams routinely encounter the same hard problems — VPC design, routing, ingress and egress, private connectivity, service exposure, address-space constraints, firewall policies, and cross-environment communication — but solve them differently depending on the deployment. We’re looking for a Senior Network Engineer to establish the architectural standards for how SGP connects to customer infrastructure and how traffic moves throughout the platform. You’ll own network architecture across a large and rapidly growing fleet of Kubernetes environments spanning AWS, Azure, and GCP, with many deployed inside customer-owned cloud accounts and networks that we do not control. The constraints vary significantly: a commercial deployment behind a customer-managed API gateway; a hub-and-spoke enterprise network where the customer assigns our address space; a GovCloud environment protected by default-deny firewall policies; or a fully air-gapped deployment with no external connectivity. The goal is not to create a bespoke network architecture for every customer. Your job is to define one clear, secure, and supportable networking model for SGP — and establish the small set of defensible variations required to operate across different clouds, customer architectures, and compliance regimes. What You'll Do Own network architecture for the SGP platform: define and enforce network standards across cloud environments (AWS, Azure, GCP) and customer deployments Design and review VPC architectures, peering, DNS, load balancing, and CDN/edge configurations (e.g., Cloudflare), grounding root-cause and tradeoff discussions in data and domain depth Bring strong technical judgment to VPN, routing, access, ingress/egress, and traffic-flow decisions Review proposed networking solutions from platform, product, and forward-deployed teams; evaluate what should and should not be introduced into the platform boundary Define the standard connectivity pattern between Scale's control plane and customer data planes (VPC peering, PrivateLink/Private Service Connect, site-to-site VPN, reverse tunnels) — and converge today's per-customer designs onto it Own the customer-boundary delivery blueprint: how code, images, and traffic cross into a customer tenant — CI/CD mirroring across org boundaries (including customer-side Azure DevOps), artifact scan gates, private registries, ingress — so new engagements configure a pattern instead of designing one Own engineer access into customer and internal environments (Tailscale/Teleport/bastion-class decisions), replacing per-engineer VPN sprawl and hand-rolled tunnels with something auditable Own the Kubernetes traffic layer: Istio/Envoy mesh and ingress, the per-cloud CNI matrix, and a portable NetworkPolicy contract that constrains egress for thousands of short-lived agent-sandbox pods running untrusted code Reduce rework by preventing one-off implementations from becoming long-term platform burden Partner with security engineering on network segmentation, zero-trust access, and compliance requirements in regulated customer environments Debug complex connectivity, latency, and traffic-flow issues across hybrid and multi-cloud deployments Document network architecture, standards, and runbooks so adjacent teams can operate confidently What We're Looking For 5+ years of network engineering experience, including designing and operating production networks in cloud environments Deep expertise in cloud networking on at least two of AWS, Azure, and GCP: VPC design, peering, Transit Gateway/hub-and-spoke topologies, private connectivity (PrivateLink, Private Service Connect), and DNS Kubernetes networking depth — CNI, ingress, NetworkPolicy, service mesh (Istio/Envoy) — this is where most of our real incidents live Strong fundamentals in TCP/IP, BGP, routing, firewalls, VPN (site-to-site and client), and TLS Experience with edge/CDN and traffic-management platforms such as Cloudflare Has defined a network standard or reference architecture that other teams adopted, and enforced it through design review Comfortable as the sole domain owner: able to collect requirements across five-plus live environments you didn't design, then converge them without breaking any Has made build-vs-adopt networking calls with vendor-support or contractual consequences in a customer's cloud Infrastructure-as-code proficiency (Terraform preferred) Familiarity with network security and compliance requirements in regulated industries (healthcare, finance, government), including environments across multiple compliance regimes (commercial, FedRAMP/GovCloud, air-gapped), is a plus Excellent communication skills — able to explain networking tradeoffs to both technical and non-technical audiences and influence decisions without direct authority Why This Role Matters Without a dedicated owner, adjacent teams are covering a domain that needs specialized expertise. You will be the point of accountability for network architecture as SGP grows — raising the quality of every deployment, unblocking confident decisions, and keeping the platform boundary clean as we scale. title: Compiler: migrate to Pliron with Rust-native structured, scheduled, and verified GPU IR
description:
Open-source contribution opportunity. Repository: harsh-nod/fe2o3. Labels: enhancement, help wanted, area:compiler. ## Goal

Build a Pliron-based fe2o3 compiler pipeline in which GPU kernels are first-class Rust items with explicit execution, capability, memory, launch and verification semantics, while supporting performance-portable GEMM, FlashAttention, MoE and other complex kernels.

The source language remains Rust. `#[kernel]` authenticates an ordinary Rust function as a GPU entry item; it does not turn the body into an IR-builder DSL or create a second algorithmic implementation. Device helpers remain ordinary Rust functions. Modules, visibility, traits, associated types, generics, const generics, ownership, borrowing, pattern matching and cross-crate monomorphization retain their normal meaning within the documented device-supported subset.

The target is not only a correct replacement for the current MIR recognizer. The target is a multi-level compiler in which:

- a generic kernel item is a Rust-level kernel family and a monomorphized kernel plus target/schedule is a concrete executable instance;
- the same executable body is consumed by ordinary rustc device extraction and the Verus proof view;
- Rust types enforce local, stable and compositional GPU invariants without exposing Pliron to users;
- fe2o3 MIR admission enforces GPU-specific rules that ordinary Rust does not express;
- Verus proves dynamic, quantified, cross-invocation, synchronization, functional and numerical properties;
- ordinary Rust can express either structured tensor algorithms or explicit low-level GPU schedules;
- algorithm semantics remain separate from tiling, mapping, pipelining and target selection;
- optimized schedules can reuse parameterized safety and functional proofs;
- target-specific AMD features remain explicit and fail closed;
- generated kernels can be qualified against pinned ROCm library baselines;
- canonical fe2o3 identities remain independent of Pliron arena and printer identity.

## Success definition

This issue is complete when fe2o3 has one production pipeline that can compile, verify, tune and execute at least one performance-qualified GEMM, fixed-shape FlashAttention forward kernel and bounded MoE routing/grouped-GEMM/combine graph without handwritten LLVM templates or raw-MIR shape recognizers.

The same release must demonstrate that a generic `#[kernel]` item defined in a library crate is monomorphized in a final crate, represented as a typed host-side kernel value, launched with borrow-checked arguments, imported from authenticated MIR metadata, admitted by the GPU Rust rules, lowered through the default Pliron pipeline and bound to its exact proof/property evidence.

Performance-qualified means the kernel has correctness, numerical, proof, resource, ISA, benchmark and target evidence tied to the exact source, algorithm, schedule, toolchain and artifact identities. A merely correct kernel is not performance-qualified.

## Non-goals

- Do not define a separate kernel language, custom control-flow syntax or user-facing Pliron builder API.
- Do not fork rustc or require upstream Rust language changes for the first production pipeline.
- Do not use a macro to translate the function body into IR-builder calls or maintain a second host/proof/device algorithm body. A macro may generate authenticated metadata, an entry shim, a typed host descriptor and a proof harness around the one body.
- Do not encode arbitrary dynamic shapes, region formulas, barrier convergence or numerical proofs into enormous Rust generic types. Those facts remain values and proof obligations.
- Do not promise that every Rust feature or standard-library API is device-executable. Unsupported reachable behavior must fail with a source-spanned call chain.
- Do not promise automatic recovery of arbitrary tensor algorithms from arbitrary optimized Rust MIR. The first structured path uses authenticated typed device operations.
- Do not make Pliron text, `Ptr<T>`, parser order or arena allocation part of a public identity.
- Do not claim that Verus proves rustc, Pliron, LLVM, LLD, ROCm, the driver or GPU hardware.
- Do not require one schedule to perform well across unrelated architectures or problem shapes.
- Do not make autotuning capable of bypassing legality, proof, target or artifact-admission checks.
- Do not remove the current reference paths until shadow comparison and performance qualification are complete.

## Current state and gap

- `dialect-mir` has a typed/serialized MIR schema and a flat `mir.*` record scaffold, but no real Pliron operations.
- `rustc-codegen-fe2o3` still uses record sketches and, for some cases, direct rustc MIR recognition.
- `fe2o3-kernel-ir` is a custom Pliron-independent SSA/CFG model with deterministic verification, semantic-operation identities, and frozen V1-V5 wire formats.
- `dialect-amdgcn` has strict AMDGPU lowering and several exact gfx942 profiles, but no Pliron AMDGCN dialect or general scheduled-kernel lowering.
- The matrix model is intentionally bounded around BF16/F32 M16N16K16 Wave64 and one XOR4 LDS profile.
- #111 covers selected hand-profiled GEMM optimizations, but there is no compiler-wide structured IR, schedule model, layout system, autotuner, or multi-kernel graph IR.
- #122-#125 are bounded FlashAttention and MoE vertical slices. They do not yet define a general performance compiler.

## Architecture principles

### 1. Treat a kernel as a first-class Rust item

`#[kernel]` marks one ordinary Rust function body with additional GPU entry semantics. The kernel has a stable item identity, concrete monomorphizations, a generated typed host descriptor, a device ABI, a launch contract and property-level evidence. Device functions are discovered by reachability and remain normal Rust functions.

The kernel surface uses Rust's existing extension mechanisms: attributes for item role, ownership/lifetimes for borrows, sealed traits and associated types for capabilities/layout compatibility, const generics for genuinely static parameters, typestate for local protocols and `unsafe` for obligations that safe APIs cannot establish. The compiler adds source-spanned MIR admission checks; it does not reinterpret normal Rust silently.

### 2. Preserve independent canonical boundaries

`fe2o3-kernel-ir` remains usable without Pliron. Existing V1-V5 wire encodings and identities remain byte-for-byte frozen.

Pliron is an in-memory transformation engine. Durable identities use fe2o3-owned canonical records:

```text
KernelItemId  = authenticated crate/item identity + generic definition
KernelInstId  = KernelItemId + concrete type/const/configuration identity
AlgorithmId   = KernelInstId + semantic operation graph + numerical contract
ScheduleId    = AlgorithmId + tiling/layout/mapping/pipeline parameters
TargetPlanId  = ScheduleId + target capabilities + legalization choices
ExecutableId  = TargetPlanId + LLVM/toolchain/object/HSACO identities
ProofInputId  = semantic snapshot + obligation/model/tool identities
```

An optimization changes `ScheduleId` without pretending to change the mathematical algorithm. Proof reuse is allowed only through an explicit parameterized refinement theorem or validated mapping.

### 3. Preserve structure until scheduling is complete

Do not immediately scalarize matmul, reductions, softmax, scans, top-k, gather/scatter or fused epilogues into loads, branches and arithmetic. Structured operations carry iteration domains, indexing maps, reduction dimensions, layouts, masks and numerical contracts.

### 4. Separate algorithm from schedule

A semantic operation describes what is computed. A schedule describes how it is tiled, distributed, staged, fused and specialized. Multiple schedules may target the same `AlgorithmId`.

### 5. Treat layout as first-class data

Logical tensor layout, global storage layout, LDS layout, wave/thread distribution, register fragment layout, masks and quantization/block-scale layout are distinct concepts and must not be collapsed into one row/column-major enum.

### 6. Treat proof as an overlay, not executable authority

`proof.*` is a solver-neutral, non-executable obligation graph referencing stable semantic IDs. It is serialized separately from executable KIR. A successful result remains an identity-bound sidecar record; there is no mutable `verified = true` operation attribute.

Rust and Verus proof state may be erased only after the compiler has recorded its identity and checked the executable/proof correspondence. Proof erasure may not create a second executable algorithm.

### 7. Make performance evidence a compiler output

Resource estimates, post-LLVM resource counts, ISA features, benchmark results and baseline identities are part of a performance record. They do not grant correctness or proof authority, but an artifact cannot be called performance-qualified without them.

## Proposed pipeline

```text
Rust crate graph
  |
  +-- #[kernel] item, normal reachable device functions
  +-- typed device capabilities and structured/scheduled APIs
  +-- launch, numerical and Verus contracts
  |
  v
rustc type/borrow checking, monomorphization, reachable MIR and FnAbi
  |
  +-- fe2o3 kernel authentication and GPU Rust MIR admission
  +-- typed host kernel descriptor and launch ABI manifest
  +-- proof erasure/source identity and Verus proof unit
  |
  v
mir.*            admitted Rust behavior under the versioned GPU Rust model
  |
  v
kernel.*         structured algorithms and numerical contracts
  |
  +------> proof.* algorithm and source/refinement obligations
  |
  v
schedule.*       tiling, fusion, mapping, specialization and pipeline plan
  |
  v
tile.*           distributed tiles, masks, regions, LDS/register layouts
  |
  +------> proof.* schedule, region, initialization and race obligations
  |
  v
gpu.*            explicit SIMT CFG, memory, barriers, atomics and epochs
  |
  +------> canonical fe2o3 Kernel IR snapshot and effect/capability closure
  |
  v
amdgcn.*         AMD instruction and target legalization
  |
  v
llvm.*           pliron-llvm dialect plus reviewed AMD extensions
  |
  v
canonical validated LLVM handoff
  |
  v
isolated pinned upstream LLVM worker -> target-machine object -> in-process LLD -> HSACO

dispatch.*       optional multi-kernel graph around admitted kernel variants
autotune.*       offline/controlled selection among already legal variants
```

The Rust-integrated model changes the frontend contract and evidence carried into this pipeline. It does not add another executable dialect or a second lowering route.

## Crate boundaries

| Crate | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `fe2o3-device` | `no_std` Rust kernel surface: `KernelContext`, address-space views, regions, tiles/fragments, masks, typestate, capabilities, structured operations and safe/unsafe device boundaries. Private constructors and sealed traits prevent forged safe values. |

Pliron dependencies must be centralized and pinned to the same exact revision across `pliron`, `pliron-derive`, and `pliron-llvm`. The first integration uses `pliron-llvm` as a dialect library with its default `llvm-sys` feature disabled. It must not introduce a second LLVM installation, build identity, linker, or artifact-authority path.

### `pliron-llvm` dialect versus machine boundary

`pliron-llvm` is adopted to avoid reimplementing ordinary LLVM operations, types, attributes, parsing, printing, and dialect conversion infrastructure. It is an internal, transient representation: its arena pointers, printer output, traversal order, and diagnostics are not canonical fe2o3 identities.

At the pinned v0.17.0 revision, the optional `llvm-sys` converter targets LLVM 22 but is not by itself a complete AMDGPU finalizer. Its reviewed surface does not own target-machine configuration or in-process LLD and does not yet carry every fe2o3-required AMDGPU calling convention, target attribute, module flag, code-object metadata, and origin/evidence field. Therefore:

- the ordinary compiler dependency graph uses `pliron-llvm` with `default-features = false`;
- `amdgcn.* -> llvm.*` lowering uses typed `pliron-llvm` operations plus the smallest reviewed fe2o3 AMD extensions or upstreamed additions needed for lossless AMDGPU semantics;
- a fe2o3-owned validator constructs a bounded canonical LLVM handoff containing the exact target, data layout, calling conventions, attributes, metadata, device-library inputs, origins, obligations, and identities;
- the isolated worker remains the sole production machine boundary and uses one measured upstream LLVM 22.1.8 build for module verification/linking/optimization, target-machine object emission, and in-process LLD HSACO linking;
- the optional `llvm-sys` converter in `pliron-llvm` is not part of the production route, including inside the worker; fe2o3 serializes only the admitted canonical V2 subset to bounded LLVM assembly, and the measured upstream LLVM 22.1.8 worker alone parses, verifies, optimizes, emits, and links those exact bytes;
- differential tests compare the dialect export and final LLVM module against the canonical handoff, and unsupported or dropped AMDGPU semantics fail closed.

This division is architectural: `pliron-llvm` owns reusable typed LLVM IR vocabulary; fe2o3 owns GPU semantics, canonical evidence and admission; pinned upstream LLVM/LLD owns machine production.

## Rust programming model

### Source-language contract

fe2o3 defines a documented GPU execution profile of Rust rather than a separate language. Normal Rust type checking, borrowing, visibility, coherence, trait selection and monomorphization happen before fe2o3 admission. A supported construct keeps its Rust meaning. An unsupported reachable construct rejects with a source span and call chain; it is never silently approximated.

The exact macro expansion and host descriptor surface are frozen by the D0 ADR, but the following semantics are normative:

- one source-level executable body per kernel;
- an authenticated kernel item and stable generic-definition identity;
- concrete type/const/cfg monomorphizations become distinct kernel instances;
- library crates may define kernels and device helpers;
- final artifact creation happens where concrete instances and target configuration are known;
- proof-only state is deterministically erased and bound to the remaining executable body;
- kernel items are not ordinary host calls or device helper calls; CPU emulation/reference execution is an explicit separate operation;
- no Pliron concepts appear in public Rust signatures.

### First-class kernel item

Illustrative source:

```rust
#[kernel]
pub fn gemm<const BM: usize, const BN: usize, const BK: usize>(
    cx: KernelContext<'_>,
    a: GlobalMatrix<'_, bf16>,
    b: GlobalMatrix<'_, bf16>,
    mut c: DisjointGlobalMatrix<'_, f32>,
) {
    let workgroup = cx.workgroup();
    let output = workgroup.output_tile::<BM, BN>(&mut c);

    let pending = workgroup.async_load::<BM, BN, BK>(&a, &b);
    let tiles = pending.wait();

    let mut acc = tiles.zero_accumulator::<Gfx942MfmaBf16>();
    acc.mma(tiles.lhs(), tiles.rhs());
    output.store(acc);
}
```

`KernelContext<'grid>` is an unforgeable compiler-provided capability and not a user-bound hardware ABI argument. It creates branded grid, workgroup, wave, lane and index values. Values branded for one launch/workgroup cannot be transferred to another through safe Rust.

The compiler-generated kernel descriptor is a typed Rust value. Illustrative host use:

```rust
let kernel = Kernel::of(gemm::<128, 128, 32>);
let launch = kernel
    .prepare(&device)?
    .grid(problem.grid())
    .bind(&a, &b, &mut c)?;

stream.submit(launch).await?;
```

The prepared/submitted value retains all referenced allocation borrows until an admitted completion event. Dropping a future or handle may cancel observation; it may not release device-visible storage early. Cross-stream use requires typed event dependencies or an explicit unsafe obligation.

### Rust-native capabilities and types

Representative source types:

```text
KernelContext<'grid>
Grid<'grid>
Workgroup<'grid, 'group>
Wave<'group, const WIDTH: usize>
Lane<'group>
ThreadIndex<'grid>

Global<'allocation, T>
Constant<'allocation, T>
Lds<'group, T, State>
Private<T>
DisjointSlice<'allocation, T>

Tile<Shape, Layout, State>
Fragment<Variant, Role, State>
Mask<Domain>
RegionPermit<'allocation, Region, Access>
AsyncToken<'group, Stage, State>
```

Safe constructors are private or sealed. Values are created only by authenticated APIs whose executable semantics, effects, required capabilities and proof contracts are registered together.

Use types for facts that are local, stable and compositional:

| Property | Rust mechanism |
|---|---|
| Allocation lifetime and host/device borrow retention | lifetimes and owning/prepared launch values |
| Read versus exclusive-write authority | shared/mutable views and branded permits |
| Address space | distinct transparent view types |
| Matrix operand role and variant compatibility | sealed traits, associated types and fragment parameters |
| Local initialization | `Uninit -> Initialized` typestate |
| Async lifecycle | `Pending -> Ready -> Reusable` typestate |
| Static shape/tile parameters | const generics where they remain ergonomic |
| Target capability availability | sealed `SupportedOn<Target>` implementations |
| Numerical mode selection | explicit policy marker bound into kernel identity |

Do not use Rust types for arbitrary dynamic coordinate formulas, all-lane facts or whole-algorithm theorems. Dynamic dimensions remain values with checked/proved witnesses.

### Three programming levels

1. **Structured Rust:** authenticated tensor/tile operations such as contraction, reduction, scan, online softmax, top-k, gather/scatter and epilogues. The compiler selects or tunes schedules.
2. **Scheduled Rust:** authors select typed tiles, layouts, pipelines and matrix variants while retaining structured algorithm identity.
3. **Explicit SIMT Rust:** authors use grid/workgroup/wave/lane capabilities, LDS, atomics and target-gated AMD operations with explicit effects and obligations.

Moving between levels does not require moving to a different language or rewriting control flow into an IR builder.

Representative structured operations:

```rust
let qk = kernel::contract(q_tile, k_tile.transpose());
let state = kernel::online_softmax_update(state, qk, mask);
let output = kernel::contract(state.probabilities(), v_tile);
```

```rust
let routes = kernel::topk::<2>(logits, TiePolicy::LowestExpert);
let counts = kernel::histogram(routes.experts());
let offsets = kernel::exclusive_scan(counts);
```

The compiler must never guess that an arbitrary loop nest is GEMM and then grant structured-operation proof or optimization authority. Pattern recognition remains inspect-only until separately validated.

### Division of verification responsibility

| Layer | Required responsibility |
|---|---|
| rustc | ordinary type/borrow/lifetime/coherence checking and concrete monomorphization |
| fe2o3 MIR admission | kernel authentication, device subset, address-space rules, capability use, token lifecycle, explicit layout conversions, unsafe obligation capture and stable source origins |
| Pliron/KIR verifiers | SSA/CFG/type/effect/capability/layout/resource well-formedness and pass pre/post verification |
| Verus | dynamic bounds, region disjointness, injectivity, cross-invocation races, convergence, async visibility, algorithm properties, numerical bounds and schedule refinement |
| lowering/artifact validators | compiler-boundary correspondence, ABI, instruction/resource/ISA and final artifact checks |

Rust ownership is affine, not fully linear: values may normally be dropped or deliberately forgotten. Proof-sensitive GPU protocol types are non-`Copy`, have controlled destruction and are additionally checked in reachable MIR. `mem::forget`, `ManuallyDrop`, transmute/raw reconstruction, invalid `Drop`, escape and failure to consume a required token reject or create an explicit unsafe/unsupported property state according to policy.

### Safe and unsafe boundaries

- Safe APIs must establish all preconditions represented by their return types and contracts.
- A target intrinsic may be safe only when target, wave, operand layout, register packing, synchronization and numerical preconditions are enforced by types/checks.
- Uncheckable raw pointer, inline assembly, external device call or target operation remains `unsafe` and emits a named obligation/trusted contract.
- An `unsafe` block never grants `Proved` evidence by itself.
- Kernel API authentication uses reserved identities/metadata, not method names, paths printed by rustc or user-implementable marker traits.

### Language compatibility contract

Maintain a versioned conformance matrix for Rust features used by kernels: functions/calls, modules, visibility, generics, const generics, traits/associated types, closures, iterators, enums/matches, references/slices, raw pointers, `unsafe`, panics/assertions, drops, statics, atomics and supported `core` APIs. Each entry is `Supported`, `Restricted`, `Lowered through contract` or `Rejected`, with positive, compile-fail and cross-crate fixtures.

Adding a restriction requires a diagnostic and documented reason. Removing a restriction requires importer, lowering, proof-policy and hardware evidence. Compiler upgrades rerun the full conformance matrix.


