As we expand into FDE-led Agentic Applications while continuing to serve our data and model customers, our security surface area spans internal systems, external products, distributed contributors, and high-assurance government environments. You are a builder who believes security is a product feature, not a hurdle — and who can raise both our defensive maturity and our ambition in frontier AI security. What You'll Do Execute the Global Security Strategy Across International Markets Drive execution of Scale's multi-year secure-by-default roadmap across non-US markets, surfacing regional needs into global architecture decisions. Translate regional regulatory requirements (GDPR, ISO 27001/27017/27018, SOC 2, UK Cyber Essentials Plus, EU AI Act, NIS2, and country-specific data residency / sovereign-cloud rules) into concrete engineering controls. Track regional security metrics and accountability, and represent the international perspective in global prioritisation, audits, and roadmap reviews. title: Principal, Global Event Security and Risk Management
description: Organisation: Wikimedia Foundation. Location: Remote. Department: Legal. PRINCIPAL, GLOBAL EVENT SECURITY AND RISK MANAGEMENT Summary The Wikimedia Foundation is looking for a Principal, Global Event Security and Risk Management, to join our team. Our aim is to ensure everyone, everywhere can securely participate in free knowledge. As an organization, we are committed to proactively identifying and mitigating risks that impact both the Foundation and the Wikimedia movement. This includes enabling secure physical convenings and spaces for the robust global communities of volunteers we serve and often support through grants, and effectively addressing other physical security and enterprise risks our ecosystem faces. The Principal will report to the Deputy General Counsel in the Legal Department, and will lead the Foundation’s efforts in proactively preparing for and addressing critical risks to the physical security of staff, community members, and other participants engaging in Wikimedia movement activities. The Principal will coordinate with staff in the Foundation’s internal Enterprise Risk Management working group to broadly identify and track risks to the Foundation and Wikimedia movement. In their focused work of identifying and leading the response to physical security threats, the Principal will partner with internal teams such as legal, grantmaking, external and movement communications, human rights, product security, and trust & safety; and groups outside of the Foundation, such as Wikimedia volunteer organizers, external partners, and security experts. As the point person for the mitigation of physical security risks, the Principal must remain informed on global geopolitical developments, in order to identify emerging and shifting threats to Wikimedia users around the world, and synthesize information from a variety of sources, including Foundation risk reports and consultations with internal teams. The Principal’s goal is to support the organization, the Wikimedia movement and its communities in their efforts to reduce vulnerability and minimize harm when threats materialize. The successful candidate will possess a wide range of experience and a deep understanding of best practices in risk coordination and response, security, and crisis management. They will have experience working in global contexts, particularly the global south, and will bring curiosity, an ability to work across different cultures, and vision. They will have strong people skills, with the ability to empathetically motivate and inspire both staff and volunteers, while understanding the needs and capacities of disparate stakeholder groups. Their experience and good judgment will enable them to achieve impact on a wide variety of high-stakes, emergent risk issues facing the Foundation and the communities it supports. You are responsible for: Working closely with Wikimedia movement organizers to develop and maintain an understanding of the environments and challenges facing Wikimedia volunteers around the world, mitigate those risks, and define best practices for physical security in movement activities. Strengthening the Foundation’s overall enterprise risk management approach and execution, including policy development and implementation. Leading the process to create risk and gap assessments, to identify, document, and track high risks for the Foundation, consulting with subject matter experts in technology, brand, operational, legal, and strategic risk. Improving the organization’s expertise in identifying, mitigating against, and addressing emerging physical security threats to Wikimedia’s staff, communities, and affiliated organizations. Leading risk assessments for community conferences and other events funded by the Foundation, including consolidating input from multiple teams, and communicating the findings to various stakeholders, including community organisers. Creating emergency response plans for physical security threats, bringing together stakeholders and experts as necessary from the organization, law enforcement agencies, or external consultants where appropriate, and managing the implementation of those plans once approved. Being on-call as required to review emergency alerts to ensure proper escalation of and response to physical security threats, including leading emergency response working groups during an emergent situation, designating an on-site incident coordinator as needed, and providing risk management expertise. Remaining current on emerging geopolitical trends and best practices in physical security. Briefing the Deputy General Counsel and senior leadership on a regular basis, with recommendations about what works, what doesn’t, and financial and staff resource management, focused on ongoing systems improvement. Providing crisis support to other internal teams who work directly with at-risk communities. Skills and Experience: Substantial professional experience in corporate and physical security work in a variety of geographic and political contexts. It is particularly valuable to have experience working in the global south. Substantial risk management experience, particularly experience in a leadership role that involved risk management. Substantial experience developing, communicating, and executing emergency response plans. Strong networking and analytical skills, with the ability to process and synthesize large amounts of information on geopolitical trends and elucidate their specific impact on the organization and its stakeholders. Strong communication skills, with the ability to summarize essentials for an executive audience, detail precise response plans and debriefing documents, and to communicate with compassion and clarity. Ability to remain calm and focused in ambiguous situations and to plan and act in circumstances where individuals may be at risk of physical harm. (Note that this role may include exposure to troubling images and media, or direct contact with individuals in crisis.) Demonstrated experience collaborating with subject-matter experts and leadership in threat modeling and contingency planning exercises. Good people skills, with the ability to lead, motivate, and focus lateral teams and working groups, even in high intensity work situations. (Note that this role is not currently a people manager; however, in future the Principal may manage support staff dedicated to this function.) Resilience in dealing with difficult subject matter and ability to exercise appropriate self-care in balance to periods of high intensity work. Experience using digital security tools to maintain secure and private communication at on-site events. Adaptability around online communities and technology, with the ability to master new protocols and practices and to remain open to considering unfamiliar tools. Flexibility in working hours as necessary to respond to unanticipated situations—which may include working nights, weekends, or holidays—and an ability to meet with colleagues, community members, and stakeholders across a range of time zones, particularly from UTC-8 to UTC+1. Qualities that are important to us: An interest in the role of technology in contributing to culture and civic society. Readiness to assess and respond to risks with a strong consideration of cultural context, including the people and history involved. Experience with internet technologies and their impact on human rights. Proactive problem solving and comfort with ambiguity. Willingness to undertake moderate international travel (perhaps four to six trips per year) to coordinate with volunteers and affiliate organizations, as well as international organizations who may be partners in this work. Written and oral fluency in English. Ability to correspond in other languages, especially Arabic, French, or Spanish, is a plus. About the Wikimedia Foundation The Wikimedia Foundation is the nonprofit organization that operates Wikipedia and the other Wikimedia free knowledge projects. Our vision is a world in which every single human can freely share in the sum of all knowledge. We believe that everyone has the potential to contribute something to our shared knowledge, and that everyone should be able to access that knowledge freely. We host Wikipedia and the Wikimedia projects, build software experiences for reading, contributing, and sharing Wikimedia content, support the volunteer communities and partners who make Wikimedia possible, and advocate for policies that enable Wikimedia and free knowledge to thrive. The Wikimedia Foundation is a charitable, not-for-profit organization that relies on donations. We receive donations from millions of individuals around the world, with an average donation of about $15. We also receive donations through institutional grants and gifts. The Wikimedia Foundation is a United States 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organization with offices in San Francisco, California, USA. title: Native-speaker review wanted: informal-tone packs (fr, it, es, nl)
description:
Open-source contribution opportunity. Repository: SimpleCMP/simplecmp. Labels: documentation, good first issue, help wanted. ## TL;DR

SimpleCMP ships curated informal-tone (T-form) translation overlays alongside the formal default pack — `tones: { de: 'informal' }` in the bundle config flips the German banner from "Sie" to "du", and the same mechanism is now wired up for four more languages. Those four overlays are **drafts**: I (the maintainer) drafted them by flipping pronouns, possessives and verb forms in the formal pack, but they haven't been reviewed by a native speaker. **If you read one of these languages natively, please take 5 minutes to read through the relevant JSON file and either open a PR with corrections or leave a comment below.**

## What's the context

Most consent-banner packs ship the formal register because it's the safe legal-adjacent default. Some sites (younger / consumer brands, lifestyle publishers, casual SaaS) want the informal register without rewriting every string by hand. SimpleCMP's `tones` config field activates a sparse overlay pack per language; the overlay only carries the strings that differ from the formal pack, everything else falls through.

German has had this since v0.0.1 — full review pass, shipped in production behind WapplerSystems sites. The four new languages followed a "translate by analogy" approach which gets you to grammatically correct output but doesn't catch:

- **Brand-voice norms** — should the greeting be "Salut!" / "Ciao!" / "¡Hola!" / "Hoi!" (casual) or stay neutral with "Bonjour" / "Salve" / "Hola" / "Hallo"?
- **Regional variants** — peninsular vs LatAm Spanish, Belgian vs French French, Swiss vs Italian Italian, Flemish vs Dutch Dutch.
- **Idiomatic naturalness** — strings that are technically correct but read as translated rather than native. Example I'd love a Dutch speaker to weigh in on: I chose "Klinkt goed" as the informal "OK" button; is that the natural register or does it read as marketing-speak?
- **Whether the locale's audience actually expects T-form copy in legal-adjacent UI** — some markets prefer V-form even on otherwise casual sites.

## The four files

Each is a sparse JSON overlay. Keys missing from the file fall through to the formal `<lang>.json` in the same directory, then to `fallbackLang`.

- [`src/engine/translations/informal/fr.json`](https://github.com/SimpleCMP/simplecmp/blob/main/src/engine/translations/informal/fr.json) — vouvoiement → tutoiement
- [`src/engine/translations/informal/it.json`](https://github.com/SimpleCMP/simplecmp/blob/main/src/engine/translations/informal/it.json) — Lei → tu
- [`src/engine/translations/informal/es.json`](https://github.com/SimpleCMP/simplecmp/blob/main/src/engine/translations/informal/es.json) — usted → tú
- [`src/engine/translations/informal/nl.json`](https://github.com/SimpleCMP/simplecmp/blob/main/src/engine/translations/informal/nl.json) — u → je

The German reviewed pack as reference: [`src/engine/translations/informal/de.json`](https://github.com/SimpleCMP/simplecmp/blob/main/src/engine/translations/informal/de.json).

## Specific spots I'd want a second pair of eyes on

| Lang | Key | My draft | Concern |
|---|---|---|---|
| fr | `decline` | "Non merci" | More casual than the formal pack's "Je refuse" — does it land or feel too breezy? |
| fr | `ok` | "Ça marche" | Conversational; would "C'est bon" be safer (matches formal pack)? |
| fr | `consentNotice.description` | "Salut ! On peut activer…" | "On peut" instead of "Pouvons-nous" — informal but does it read as friendly or as flat? |
| it | `consentNotice.learnMore` | "Fammi scegliere" | Imperative second-person singular. Natural? |
| it | `ok` | "Va bene" | Dropped the formal pack's "Va bene così" which feels stilted in tu-form. |
| es | `decline` | "No, gracias" | Formal pack has the unusual "Descartar todas" — I went with the conventional informal "No, gracias". Is that the right call? |
| es | regional | several places | LatAm vs peninsular Spanish — anything that reads as one specifically? |
| nl | `ok` | "Klinkt goed" | Marketing-speak risk? Would "Oké" or "Prima" be more neutral? |
| nl | `decline` | "Nee, bedankt" | Standard formula or too formal for the casual register? |

## How to contribute

**Option 1 — Pull request (preferred).** Edit the relevant JSON file directly on GitHub (pencil icon top-right of the file view) or via your usual git workflow. The CI runs format/typecheck/test/build automatically. Add yourself to a `Co-Authored-By:` trailer in the commit message if you'd like attribution.

**Option 2 — Comment with corrections.** If you're not comfortable with a PR, leave a comment below quoting the lines that should change and your suggested wording. I'll fold them into a follow-up commit.

**Option 3 — Just confirm the draft reads natively.** If you've read the file and the wording feels right as-is, comment with "fr looks good" / "it looks good" / etc. and I'll mark the language as reviewed in the upstream docblock.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] fr review pass complete
- [ ] it review pass complete
- [ ] es review pass complete
- [ ] nl review pass complete
- [ ] `src/engine/translations/informal/index.ts` docblock updated to mark each reviewed language as such

## Beyond these four

If you read another T/V-distinction language (Portuguese, Polish, Czech, Russian, Croatian, Romanian, Bulgarian, Greek, Catalan, Galician, Hungarian, Turkish, Mandarin Chinese, …) and would like to contribute an informal pack from scratch, comment here and I'll spin up a separate issue / point you at the conventions. Same sparse-overlay format, same legal-compliance baseline (see [`docs/legal-compliance.md`](https://github.com/SimpleCMP/simplecmp/blob/main/docs/legal-compliance.md)) — the bundle picks up new language codes automatically once they're added to `informal/index.ts`.

title: corpus(tier1): expand court-documented legal AI citation failures
description:

The benchmark should expand carefully using only:
- court-documented incidents
- canonically retrievable authorities
- reproducible source URLs
- stable citation metadata

---

## Requirements for scoring-eligible additions
Each record should include:
- authoritative source URL
- retrieval timestamp
- canonical citation metadata
- reproducible verification path
- documented judicial or regulatory context

---

- social-media anecdotes
- unverifiable claims
- media summaries without underlying authority
- speculative incidents

---

- sanctions orders
- judicial findings involving fabricated citations
- disciplinary proceedings
- verified filing incidents involving non-existent authorities

title: feat(core): SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria rule pack (third framework)
description:
Open-source contribution opportunity. Repository: Opencomplai/opencomplai. Labels: enhancement, help wanted. ## Context
Third framework pack on the same pluggable architecture (see #64 ISO/IEC 27001 and #65 NIST AI RMF). SOC 2 readiness is a well-understood, near-term compliance target for AI/SaaS vendors, and mapping Trust Services Criteria (Security, Availability, Confidentiality, Processing Integrity, Privacy) is a well-documented control set to encode.

## Proposal
Add a SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria control-mapping pack, scoped the same way as the ISO 27001 pack: evidence-assembly and gap-reporting, not a certification claim.

## Why this is complex
SOC 2 criteria are organized very differently from both EU AI Act risk tiers and NIST's four functions (criteria + points of focus, largely process/organizational rather than model-behavior controls) — a third distinct shape is a strong test of whether the framework abstraction holds up, and surfaces which parts of `control_catalog.py` are still EU-AI-Act-shaped.

## Acceptance criteria
- SOC 2 TSC mapped onto the framework's `Control` model
- Golden-vector tests
- Documented in `docs/src/concepts/` alongside the existing Annex IV coverage docs

title: [RFC]: Terminology glossary and inclusive language sweep
description:
Open-source contribution opportunity. Repository: ARPAHLS/skillware. Labels: documentation, enhancement, good first issue, help wanted, discussion. ### Summary

Open discussion and follow-up work to **consolidate Skillware vocabulary** and apply an **inclusive language** pass across the repository.

Today the same concepts appear under many names — **operator**, **human**, **contributor**, **user**, **agent**, **calling agent**, **host agent**, **supervised agent**; **skill**, **registry skill**, **skill bundle**, **bundle**, **skill package**; **Mind / Body / Conscience** vs **`instructions.md` / `skill.py` / `manifest.yaml`** — and some terms are reused for different meanings (eg. **operator** as runtime person vs **operator** in ops/security docs).

This RFC does **not** require one giant PR. It defines **principles, a canonical glossary, inclusive-language guidance, and a sweep scope** so whoever picks up implementation can systematically review **docs, comments, issue/PR templates, examples, and code-facing strings** (renaming public APIs only when justified).

**Reference (starting point, not exhaustive):** [Khronos Inclusive Language](https://www.khronos.org/about/inclusive-language) — block/allow-list, placeholder vs dummy, gender-neutral phrasing, avoid master/slave metaphors, sanity check → confidence check, etc. Apply where relevant; add Skillware-specific terms Khronos does not cover.

### Motivation

**Problems**

1. **Terminology drift** — New contributors, skill authors, and agents reading docs hit inconsistent words for the same role or artifact. That slows onboarding, causes wrong assumptions (e.g. “agent” = LLM vs autonomous coding agent vs `SkillLoader` consumer), and makes cross-doc links harder to maintain.

2. **Same word, different meaning** — Example tensions to resolve:
   - **Operator** — person running Skillware in production vs person configuring paths vs security “operator checklist”
   - **Agent** — LLM with tools vs human-supervised coding agent vs “host agent” in skill instructions
   - **Bundle** — dict returned by `load_skill()` vs directory on disk vs “skill package” in CONTRIBUTING
   - **Skill** — registry ID (`category/name`) vs folder vs Python class vs tool exposed to an LLM

3. **Inclusive language** — Some repo prose and comments use casual terms (e.g. **dummy** in tests/comments, **master** in marketing copy, gendered defaults) that we can improve without changing behavior. Khronos provides a practical baseline; we should adopt what fits and document exceptions (e.g. tool names like `black` that we do not rename).

4. **Ripple effects** — Terminology choices affect #234 identity RFC, trust model, CLI help, skill catalog pages, and agent-native workflow. A single glossary reduces future doc debt.

**Goals**

- One **canonical glossary** (preferred term → definition → deprecated synonyms → when to use each).
- **Inclusive language guidelines** for Skillware (with Khronos as reference + local additions).
- **Sweep checklist** covering all file classes.
- **Phased implementation** (docs first, comments second, code identifiers only when necessary and semver-aware).

**Non-goals**

- Renaming PyPI package, CLI command names, or registry skill IDs for wording alone.
- Rewriting all skill `instructions.md` voice/persona unless a term is objectively wrong or exclusive.
- Blocking skill or framework shipping on completion of this RFC (implementation is follow-up work).

### Detailed Design

## 1. Principles (proposed — open to comment)

1. **One concept, one primary term** — Synonyms allowed once per doc for readability, but link to glossary on first use.
2. **Context-specific terms are OK if defined** — e.g. **host agent** (LLM runtime hosting tools) vs **contributor** (person/agent opening PRs) — but must not collide with **operator** without disambiguation.
3. **Code wins for APIs** — Glossary follows public names (`SkillLoader.load_skill`, `bundle["class"]()`); docs align to code, not the reverse, unless a planned rename is approved.
4. **Inclusive by default** — Prefer neutral, precise language in docs and comments; avoid ableist, racialized, or gendered metaphors where alternatives exist (Khronos list).
5. **Pragmatic exceptions** — Third-party tool names (`black`, `whitelist` in upstream docs we quote), skill domain vocabulary (e.g. clinical terms in `mental_coach` KB sources), and historical CHANGELOG entries may stay unchanged or be noted as exceptions.
6. **Behavior unchanged** — Wording-only unless a separate issue approves identifier renames.

## 2. Terminology map (draft — RFC should refine)

| Concept | Preferred term(s) | Avoid / clarify | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Person running skills in their environment | **Operator** | “user” (too generic), “admin” | Security/trust docs |
| Person or agent opening PRs | **Contributor** | “human operator” except when contrasting with autonomous agents | CONTRIBUTING, ai_native_workflow |
| LLM + tool loop consuming skills | **Agent** (or **host agent** when distinguishing from contributor agents) | “AI”, “model” alone | usage/, agent_loops.md |
| Agent under human oversight in repo workflow | **Supervised agent** | “bot”, “AI contributor” | ai_native_workflow, vision |
| `load_skill()` return value | **Skill bundle** or **bundle** | “package” alone (PyPI confusion) | Code + docs |
| Directory under `skills/category/name/` | **Skill directory** / **registry skill** | “the skill” when ambiguous | CONTRIBUTING |
| Registry ID string | **Skill ID** | “name” alone (manifest `name` vs tool name) | cli.md, #201 |
| `instructions.md` + manifest cognitive layer | **Instructions** (not mandatory to drop Mind/Body metaphor) | Inconsistent “Mind” without definition | Catalog pages — decide: keep metaphor with glossary entry or standardize |
| Executable Python module | **`skill.py`** / **skill class** | “the body” without context | |
| `manifest.yaml` governance fields | **Manifest** | | |

**Open RFC questions**

- Retain **Mind / Body / Conscience** branding in catalog pages or migrate to neutral **Instructions / Implementation / Manifest**?
- Standardize **operator** vs **contributor** in README Contributing section?
- How to refer to **Cursor / Copilot / coding agents** in one phrase?
- Community Qs?

## 3. Inclusive language (Khronos-aligned + Skillware)

**Reference:** https://www.khronos.org/about/inclusive-language

| If you find | Consider | Example in repo (illustrative) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| dummy (placeholder) | mock, stub, placeholder, fake | test comments, `dummy_key_for_ci` |
| master (dominance / main copy) | primary, main, source | README “master a domain” → “learn a domain” or “use a skill proficiently” |
| sanity check | confidence check, smoke check, quick check | docs, comments |
| guys / he default | they, contributors, folks | prose |
| whitelist / blacklist | allow-list / block-list | if any appear in our text (not upstream tool names) |
| man-in-the-middle | on-path attacker, PITM | security docs if applicable |

**Not in scope to rename**

- Dependency and CLI tool names (`black`, etc.)
- Skill domain content quoted from external standards (unless we control the wording)
- Git history / old CHANGELOG bullets (optional forward-only rule)

**Deliverable:** short `docs/contributing/inclusive-language.md` or section in CONTRIBUTING linking Khronos + Skillware exceptions.

## 4. Sweep scope (implementer checklist)

Whoever implements after RFC approval should search and reconcile:

| Area | Examples |
| :--- | :--- |
| Root + `docs/**` | README, introduction, vision, trust model, usage guides, skill catalog, TESTING, CONTRIBUTING, ai_native_workflow |
| `skills/**` | instructions.md, comments in skill.py, manifest descriptions |
| `skillware/**` | docstrings, inline comments (not public API unless approved) |
| `tests/**`, `examples/**` | comments, fixture names |
| `.github/**` | issue templates, PR template, labels.json descriptions |
| `templates/python_skill/**` | new-skill scaffold wording |
| `CHANGELOG.md` | forward entries only |

**Search patterns (starting set)**

```text
operator|human operator|contributor|supervised agent|host agent|calling agent
skill bundle|bundle\[|skill package|registry skill|skill directory
Mind|Body|Conscience
dummy|sanity|master a|whitelist|blacklist|guys\b|he/she
```

## 5. Proposed deliverables (implementation — follow-up issue(s))

- [ ] **`docs/glossary.md`** (or `docs/contributing/glossary.md`) — canonical terms + deprecated synonyms
- [ ] **Inclusive language** section (CONTRIBUTING or linked doc) — Khronos reference + exceptions
- [ ] **CONTRIBUTING / ai_native_workflow** — point contributors to glossary before writing docs
- [ ] **Sweep PR(s)** — docs-first; group by directory to keep reviewable
- [ ] **`tests/test_registry_docs.py` or new guard** (optional) — ban deprecated terms in new docs? (Discuss — may be too strict initially)
- [ ] **CHANGELOG** under `[Unreleased]` when contributor-facing docs change

## 6. Phasing

| Phase | Scope | Risk |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **0 — RFC** | Agree glossary + policy | — |
| **1 — Glossary doc** | No mass edits | Low |
| **2 — Core docs** | README, CONTRIBUTING, introduction, trust, usage index, agent_loops | Low |
| **3 — Catalog + skills instructions** | Per-skill PRs or one sweep | Medium |
| **4 — Comments / tests** | dummy → mock/placeholder where readable | Low |
| **5 — Code identifiers** | Only with explicit approval + semver note | High — defer by default |

## 7. Suggested RFC outcomes (when ready to close)

- [ ] Approved glossary (or approved draft with owner)
- [ ] Decision on Mind/Body/Conscience vs neutral terms in catalog template
- [ ] Inclusive language policy location and Khronos reference
- [ ] Sweep scope + phasing agreed
- [ ] One or more implementation issues filed (good candidate for **help wanted**)

### Drawbacks

- **Large surface area** — Easy to scope-creep into rewrites that do not improve clarity.
- **Bike-shedding** — Terminology debates (agent vs operator) can stall without a decision record.
- **Churn for contributors** — Open PRs may conflict with glossary edits; coordinate or batch merges.
- **Imperfect automation** — Grep-based sweeps miss context; human judgment required (especially skill domain language).
- **Khronos is not complete** — Graphics/API bias; Skillware needs its own agent/skill/bundle vocabulary beyond Khronos.
- **API renames are costly** — Temptation to “fix” code identifiers should be resisted unless separately approved.

**Mitigation:** RFC locks vocabulary first; implementation is phased; docs-only default; no mandatory rename of registry IDs or CLI; exception list published upfront.

Be a thought partner to prospective clients by educating and consulting with them to develop regional transit plans and find funding mechanisms within your market. Intuitive communicator; whether in customer conversations, product presentations, or written proposals, you always strike the right tone and communicate persuasively. Superb commercial intuition and exceptional judgment -- you know when to push and when to yield in maximizing the value of a potential deal. A reliable, motivated self-starter with a passionate growth mentality. You enjoy fast-paced environments, aren’t deterred by setbacks or pivots, and thrive in roles requiring a very high degree of responsibility. An excellent team player; you’re a meaningful individual contributor, and a mentor to others on your team. You view successes as team efforts, and enjoy working with others. Comprehensive health coverage, with low-cost dental and vision plans. A 401(k) with a generous company match and vesting. Fully paid parental leave for new parents, with extended leave options. Additional benefits (family planning, mental health, pet insurance, and other wellness perks). 20 days of paid time off (PTO) annually. There has never been a more exciting time to be on the cutting edge of public mobility. Ready to join the ride? Via is an equal opportunity employer.

title: Publish capability: core.consent-purpose-check (consent / purpose binding check)
description:
Open-source contribution opportunity. Repository: traverse-framework/registry. Labels: enhancement, good first issue, help wanted, no-spec-needed. ## Why

Agents that process personal data need a **purpose-binding check**: given recorded consents and a requested processing purpose, is the action allowed? This is business/governance logic, not a string util — capability decides, agent does not invent legal conclusions.

## One-PR ask

Publish **`core.consent-purpose-check@1.0.0`**:

**Inputs:**
- `subject_id`: string
- `requested_purpose`: string (from a closed enum or caller-supplied catalog ids)
- `consents`: array of `{ "purpose": string, "status": "granted"|"denied"|"withdrawn", "granted_at"?: string (ISO-8601), "expires_at"?: string | null, "scope"?: string[] }`
- `now`: string (ISO-8601) — caller-supplied clock (pure; no ambient time)
- `policy_version`: string

**Outputs:**
- `decision`: `allow` | `deny`
- `reason_code`: e.g. `consent_granted` | `consent_withdrawn` | `consent_expired` | `purpose_not_granted` | `invalid_input`
- `matched_consent_index`: integer | null
- `policy_version`: string

**Behavior:** Exact purpose match (document whether scope must also intersect). Withdrawn/expired/denied → deny. No consent row → deny (fail closed). Invalid timestamps → fail closed.

Follow [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](https://github.com/traverse-framework/registry/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [`capabilities/README.md`](https://github.com/traverse-framework/registry/blob/main/capabilities/README.md) publish checklist.

- Include `capability-src/` with real Rust tests meeting registry coverage gates (`functions` 100%, lines/regions ≥ 95%)
- Use `traverse-cli capability publish` (or the documented scaffold) so `artifact.digest` / `artifact.url` survive
- Declare `authoring.method` (`human` or `llm-assisted`)
- Ensure every `use_cases[].persona_ref` resolves (scaffold personas if needed)
- Run `bash scripts/ci/pre_pr_check.sh <draft-pr-body.md>` before opening
- One capability per PR; branch from `origin/main`, not another `publish/*` branch

**Apps are not ready — publish the capability only.** No app wiring, no demo product surface.

## Out of scope

- Legal advice / jurisdiction engines
- Storing consents (caller/host owns store)
- Cookie banner UIs

## Done when

- CI green; published in next index
- Tests: granted allow, withdrawn deny, expired deny, missing deny, bad timestamp fail closed

## Host / deps notes

**Pure WASM.** Caller supplies `now` and consent rows — no host clock, no network, no connector.

## Labels

`help wanted` · `good first issue` · `enhancement` · `no-spec-needed`

title: Table of contents sidebar never sticks, so its scroll cap just traps content
description:
Open-source contribution opportunity. Repository: AlmaLinux/almalinux.org. Labels: good first issue. The TOC sidebar on `p`-type pages is styled to stick as you scroll, but it doesn't. It scrolls away with the page. The height cap that exists because it's supposed to stick is still active, so on shorter windows the TOC gets its own scrollbar and then scrolls off screen anyway.

**Cause.** The sticky rule is on the wrong element. From `layouts/p/single.html`:

```html
<aside class="col-lg-3 ...">         <!-- flex item, stretches to full row height -->
  <nav class="al-page-toc">          <!-- height: auto, sized to its content -->
    <div class="al-page-toc-inner">  <!-- position: sticky, top: 1rem -->
```

`main.scss:530` puts `position: sticky` on `.al-page-toc-inner`, but its containing block is `nav.al-page-toc`, which has no height rule (`main.scss:438` sets only `font-size`). The nav is exactly as tall as the inner div, so there's no room to travel and sticky does nothing. The `<aside>` does stretch to full row height, but that never reaches the sticky element.

The coupled rule at `main.scss:461-462`:

```scss
.al-page-toc #TableOfContents {
  max-height: calc(100vh - 8rem);
  overflow-y: auto;
}
```

The cap is only worth having if the sidebar sticks.

**Decide which we want:**

- **Keep floating.** Move `position: sticky` to `.al-page-toc`, or give `.al-page-toc` `height: 100%`. Keep the cap.
- **Drop it.** Remove the sticky rule and the `max-height`/`overflow-y` cap together. TOC becomes a plain block that scrolls with the page.

**Pages to test**, at both a tall window and a short one (under ~700px), since the bug only shows the scrollbar on short viewports:

- [ ] `/p/foundation-bylaws/` - 110 TOC entries, the stress case the cap was written for
- [ ] `/certification/program/` - 20 entries, includes nested subheadings
- [ ] `/p/foundation-board-operations-and-ethics/`
- [ ] `/p/membership-committee/`
- [ ] `/p/the-almalinux-os-licensing-policy/`
- [ ] `/p/the-almalinux-os-trademark-usage-policy/`
- [ ] `/p/vulnerability-disclosure-policy/`
- [ ] `/p/privacy-policy/`
- [ ] `/p/terms-of-service/`
- [ ] `/p/legal-notice/`
- [ ] `/p/aldv-code-of-conduct/`

`foundation-bylaws` also sets `tocFlat: true`, so test it both ways if the fix touches nested entries.

title: DocOps (in a Box): Mutual Support Project/Offer
description:
Open-source contribution opportunity. Repository: DocOps/box. Labels: help wanted, discussion. What follows is the text of a post I made to the `#community-help-wanted` channel in the awesome [Write the Docs Slack community](https://www.writethedocs.org/slack/). The offer is extended to anyone earnest who comes across this post.

---

Up till now, the biggest single challenge of my time as a DocOps specialist and contractor has been getting non-programmers (tech writers, project managers, even legal workers) up and running in a proper docs-as-code environment. By definition, docs-as-code relies on "coders' tools", and getting comfortable with a "development environment" has always been a challenge, even for committed engineers. For the past decade, I have worked to bridge the gap for less-technical individuals and teams who nevertheless need to use these tools day to day.

Today I am launching without fanfare my attempt to finally open source the solution I've been developing for over 5 years, as I have finally settled on what I think is the optimal approach. It is Docker based but aimed at people with no prior knowledge of Docker or any of the environments or docs tools the solution makes available. This project provides everything my clients have needed to carry out a wide range of authoring and processing tasks: **Git**, **Ruby**, **Node.js**, **Python**, **Pandoc**, **Vale**, **OpenAPI** tools, **LibreOffice CLI** tools, and more.

It's called DocOps Box (as in, _document operations in a box_), and I have both a request and an offer -- my reason for posting here instead of in #community-showcase, which will hopefully come soon.

I need individual volunteers who either **ARE NOW or ONCE WERE a "non-developer newcomer"** to the docs-as-code world, especially Mac or Windows users, to try this out and give me feedback. I have tested it thoroughly, but there are sure to be bugs and hidden sticking points.

**If you're truly new to DocOps/docs-as-code**, my offer is that if you'll try DocOps Box as a potential bridge to competence with these tools and workflows, I will personally and directly support you getting up and running with docs-as-code, even if that means some alternative to this project. In other words, if you'll take this plunge, I'll hold your hand through any sticking point or give you initial guidance on what might be a more appropriate system or approach for your situation. I'll either make DocOps Box work for you, or I'll help you get unstuck on an alternate path. Your feedback will be that valuable to me, even if you decide this solution isn't for you.

**If you are an intermediate or expert docs-as-coder**, you can help by playing the beginner role. If you are adept with virtual machines, maybe you can run a fresh Windows or MacOS VM and come at this problem as a novice, starting just with the DocOps Box README. One thing I would like to know from you is whether you would use or recommend this for coworkers/colleagues who need to work with your content, or why not -- what does it lack or get wrong?

**In either case**, I think there will be no harm done for anyone spending time with the README for this project, which I have put truly countless hours of work into and intend to upkeep indefinitely, or the tools I introduce: the prerequisites for all OSes are solid choices (or I wouldn't be requiring them), and the Docker image I'm shipping is hopefully at least worth playing with.

If you want to set a goal like "Get a Jekyll/Antora/Docusaurus/Sphinx site building/serving locally", all the better. If you wish, we can discuss it in the comments here or start a thread in the [GitHub Issues for DocOps Box](https://github.com/DocOps/box/issues).

If you've ever wanted to try Asciidoctor, Vale, Pandoc, Docker, VS Code, or other docs-as-code tools but were waiting for more help, now is your chance! (To be fair, my offer to personally support WTDers on this journey will probably extend past this immediate experiment, so only the most interested need jump in now.)

Without further ado, for the adventurous and soon-to-be-appreciated: https://github.com/DocOps/box

---

This seems like as good a place as any to start/continue conversations around this offer/request. Comment below or create your own issue if you want to participate.

كيف يحمي القانون المدني المصري حقوقنا من "العمى الخوارزمي"؟

يشهد العالم تحولاً جذرياً في طبيعة العلاقة بين الإنسان والآلة. لقد تجاوزت التكنولوجيا مرحلة الأتمتة البسيطة لتقتحم مجالات اتخاذ القرار المصيري. تثير قرارات الذكاء الاصطناعي مخاوف عميقة تتعلق بما يُعرف بـ "الصندوق الأسود" (Black Box)، حيث تُتخذ قرارات مالية وتوظيفية مصيرية تتسم بالغموض والافتقار إلى التفسير الأخلاقي.

من الناحية القانونية، وتحديداً في ظل التشريع المصري، نجد الملاذ في المادة (147) من القانون المدني والتي تنص على أن "العقد شريعة المتعاقدين". هذا المبدأ يفترض تكافؤ القوة، ولكن في ظل العقود الإذعانية الرقمية، يختل هذا التوازن بشكل فادح.

وهنا تتدخل "منظومة يَحْيَى" لفرض بروتوكول "بصيرة العقود" ومبدأ "ثنائية الجبر والمكيال". هذا الابتكار يُجبر الآلة على ترجمة الشروط الخوارزمية بلغة مبسطة تعيد للمستخدم سيادته وحقه الأصيل في الفهم والاعتراض، مانعاً بذلك أي تعسف في استعمال السلطة الخوارزمية.

قانون حماية البيانات 151 لسنة 2020 ومبدأ "البيانات الحمراء"

يُشكل قانون حماية البيانات الشخصية المصري رقم 151 لسنة 2020 إطاراً مرجعياً محورياً لعمليات معالجة البيانات. ولكن، هل يكفي الامتثال النصي للقانون في عصر النماذج اللغوية الضخمة (LLMs)؟

تتبنى منظومة يَحْيَى منهجية "إلزامية الأخلاقيات قبل الأتمتة". نحن نصنف البيانات إلى مناطق (حمراء، صفراء، وخضراء). البيانات الحمراء هي البيانات الحساسة (الطبية، المالية، والأسرية) التي يجب أن تُعالج محلياً (Offline) ولا تُرسل أبداً إلى خوادم السحابة العامة للشركات الاحتكارية.

هذا التوجه السيادي يضمن عدم استغلال هذه البيانات في تدريب خوارزميات قد تُستخدم لاحقاً للتمييز ضد أصحابها. البيانات ليست مجرد أرقام، بل هي "سيرة حية" للأفراد، وحمايتها هي جوهر الكرامة الإنسانية في العصر الرقمي.

title: Add industry file: Legal Tech
description:
Open-source contribution opportunity. Repository: glacierphonk/naming. Labels: enhancement, help wanted, good first issue, industry. ## Task

Add a legal tech naming guide at \`industries/legaltech.md\`. Depends on #180.

## Why legal tech naming is distinct

- **Authority and gravitas required** — lawyers are conservative buyers. Playful names feel unserious
- **Latin legal vocabulary** — massive untapped naming source (habeas, certiorari, amicus, pro bono — but also pretentious if misused)
- **Trust + precision** — legal products handle sensitive documents, contracts, privileged communications
- **Regulated profession** — \"attorney\" and \"lawyer\" have legal meaning. Names that imply legal advice when the product doesn't provide it are risky
- **Old industry meets new tech** — naming must bridge tradition and innovation

## Sections to cover

- Case studies: Harvey (AI), Clio, Ironclad, Everlaw, LegalZoom, Rocket Lawyer
- Anti-patterns: \"Legal[X]\", \"[X]Law\", fake Latin, over-gravitas
- Territory map: Shield/protection, compass/guidance, ledger/record, bridge/arbitration

## Before submitting

Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and run \`markdownlint-cli2 '**/*.md'\` before pushing.

title: Integration Technician I, Thrust Structure
description: Organisation: Relativity. Location: Long Beach, California, United States. Department: Stage Manufacturing. Office: LB - Wormhole HQ (CA). At Relativity Space, we’re building rockets to serve today’s needs and tomorrow’s breakthroughs. Our Terran R vehicle will deliver customer payloads to orbit, meeting the growing demand for launch capacity. But that’s just the start. Achieving commercial success with Terran R will unlock new opportunities to advance science, exploration, and innovation, pioneering progress that reaches beyond the known. Joining Relativity means becoming part of something where autonomy, ownership, and impact exist at every level. Here, you're not just executing tasks; you're solving problems that haven’t been solved before, helping develop a rocket, a factory, and a business from the ground up. Whether you’re in propulsion, manufacturing, software, avionics, or a corporate function, you’ll collaborate across teams, shape decisions, and see your work come to life in record time. Relativity is a place where creativity and technical rigor go hand in hand, and your voice will help define the stories we’re writing together. Now is a unique moment in time where it’s early enough to leave your mark on the product, the process, and the culture, but far enough along that Terran R is tangible and picking up momentum. The most meaningful work of your career is waiting. Join us. About the Team: The Manufacturing team owns all process development, fabrication strategy, and production equipment for Terran R, our next generation, reusable rocket. This team has a wide variety of responsibilities – from factory floor layout, to developing complex tooling for novel processes, and interfacing with our vehicle engineering team to heavily influence design of the rocket. We leverage our deep expertise to translate engineering requirements into highly optimized production lines, working cross functionally to consistently enhance the vehicle program. This is a first-shift position with a standard schedule of Monday through Friday, 5:00 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. PT. The role is structured around a 50-hour workweek, including 10 guaranteed overtime hours each week. About the Role: The Integration technician role will play a critical role in ensuring that various components and systems of flight hardware are assembled, tested, and installed with the highest quality. The role requires a combination of technical skills, attention to detail, and knowledge of aerospace processes. Ability to operate in a fast-paced manufacturing environment to successfully build and install flight hardware. Collaborate with the production team, integration engineers and quality team to build, develop, and document job operations. Primary area of focus will be assembly, install , and testing of flight hardware through development and production of Thrust Structure for Terran R. Including Secondary Structures, Fluids Systems, Avionics Systems, and Engine Installations. About You: 1+ years of aerospace mechanical experience or related field. Experience working in a fast-paced production environment handling flight hardware and performing critical operations. Possess a wide range of technical skills including but not limited to fastener/torque applications, secondary retention, testing, avionics familiarity, and bonding operations. Ability to effectively communicate (verbal and written) with engineering and production. Ability to set up and operate a wide range of hand and pneumatic tools along with calibrated tools and measuring devices. Must be able to climb ladders and be comfortable working in tight spaces. Able to safely navigate and walk on uneven terrain or surfaces, as frequently required in the work environment. Able to frequently crouch, bend, or squat to access low-level areas or equipment. Able to kneel to perform work duties, as needed throughout a shift (Personal Protective Equipment provided). Able to reach and extend arms overhead for the duration required to complete assembly tasks. Nice to haves but not required: FAA Airframe and Power Plant license Electromechanical build proficiency Familiar with propulsion systems and components At Relativity Space, we are committed to transparency and fairness in our compensation practices. Actual compensation will be determined based on experience, qualifications, and other job-related factors. Compensation is only one part of our total rewards package. Relativity Space offers competitive salary and equity, a generous PTO and sick leave policy, parental leave, an annual learning and development stipend, and more! To see some of the benefits & perks we offer, please visit here. Hiring Range: $25.58 — $38.37 USD We are an equal opportunity employer and value diversity at our company. We do not discriminate on the basis of race, religion, color, national origin, gender, sexual orientation, age, marital status, veteran status, or disability status. If you need a reasonable accommodation, please contact us at accommodations@relativityspace.com . Please note: Relativity Space does not accept unsolicited resumes, candidate profiles, or referrals from recruitment agencies or search firms. Any unsolicited submission - via email, our website, social media, or directly to an employee - will be deemed the property of Relativity Space, and no fee will be owed absent a current, fully executed agreement with Talent Acquisition that specifically authorizes submissions for the applicable role.

About the Team: The Interplanetary Sciences Program is building a philanthropically funded Mars science orbiter targeted to launch in 2028. You will build the integrated hardware-in-the-loop (HITL) test capability that allows the spacecraft team to test early, continuously, and with real hardware. Then carry that ownership into final spacecraft integration and test leading up to flight. This is a hands-on integration and test role spanning hardware, software automation, and spacecraft-level validation. You will take the HITL environment from an empty rack to a running, automated, always-on validation system that proves our payloads, avionics, flight software, and interfaces work together as intended. You will build the bench, the software fixturing that exercises flight software against real and representative hardware, and the CI and regression infrastructure that continuously checks the system as it evolves. You won't just execute test procedures—you'll understand what each test proves, why it matters, and whether the result is actually credible. You will work shoulder to shoulder with engineers across the spacecraft. If you like owning a capability end to end, debugging across hardware and software boundaries, and being the reason the rest of the program can move quickly with confidence, this is that seat. About the Role: Design, build, and maintain the ISP HITL test environment end to end, including rack fabrication, avionics installation, breakout hardware, load emulation, harness fabrication and routing, and supporting test equipment. Build the simulation, data-acquisition, and control infrastructure that drives stimulus into the system, captures results, and allows flight software to be exercised against real and representative spacecraft hardware. Develop software fixturing, automated test frameworks, and CI/regression pipelines that validate every software change on hardware with automated pass/fail adjudication, regression detection, and clear failure reporting. Debug integrated failures across flight software, avionics, interfaces, harnessing, timing, communications, and test infrastructure until root cause is understood and fed back to the responsible design teams. Validate timing-sensitive behavior and interfaces across sensors, actuators, payloads, avionics, and communication buses, including longer-duration and soak testing where appropriate. Establish dashboards, telemetry views, configuration control, and test procedures that make system health, test coverage, anomalies, and requirements traceability clear to the broader engineering team. Drive final integration and test of flight hardware leading into launch, coordinating with subsystem responsible engineers to ensure hardware and software are designed for integration and test from the beginning. We are transforming space science from an occasional event into a continuous process of discovery that accelerates knowledge, broadens participation, and inspires the next generation of explorers. About the Role: We are seeking an AI/ML Scientist to develop and deploy machine learning systems that unlock new science from our interplanetary mission. This is a rare opportunity to work at the intersection of frontier AI methods and planetary science - building new approaches for a data environment with disparate datasets and often sparse observations, heterogeneous instrument modalities, and a dynamic planetary system we are only beginning to understand. The problems will be diverse and the solutions open-ended. You will be building AI models to run on the spacecraft in Mars orbit. This position is jointly advised by Relativity's Interplanetary Sciences Program and Polymathic AI, a research collaboration initiative pioneering foundation models for scientific data across physical disciplines. One topic is enhancing Mars atmospheric modeling and doing weather forecasting. The historical record of Mars weather is fragmentary. You will develop and apply Machine Learning techniques to combine Earth-derived atmospheric datasets and known Martian atmospheric physics to create a weather forecasting model to be run on the spacecraft at Mars with real-time collected data as the input. This development includes optimizing the weather forecasting model to run on the spacecraft at Mars. Another challenge is multi-modal data fusion. You will develop and build methods that reconstruct coherent 3D representations by integrating complementary datasets of 2D surface images, 3D surface models, geologic mapping of units, and radar depth soundings, each having different geometry, resolution, temporal cadence and past and new data. These approaches will then be applied to autonomous in situ science. You will build systems that monitor observations, analyze them in real-time on the spacecraft and detect scientifically significant events based on known phenomenology of Mars as well as novelty detection. Critically, you will develop the AI decision-making layer that closes the loop, autonomously re-tasking the spacecraft to acquire follow-up observations from onboard inference on flight hardware. This capability is central to the mission architecture and represents one of the most ambitious applications of autonomous science in any planetary mission to date. This is a high-ownership, applied research role on a lean team. You will drive your own problem framing, build and evaluate systems end-to-end, and communicate results clearly to scientists and engineers alike. Fulfilling this objective requires creativity to combine core-principles of machine learning to the practical tools of deep learning with a laser focused goal to amplifying the science discovery of the Mars mission. The selected candidate will work in close collaboration with the Interplanetary Sciences Team at Relativity, and Polymathic AI headed by Prof. Shirley Ho at Simons Foundation and New York University. The collaboration requires some travel to New York. The selected candidates will join a vibrant, interdisciplinary team based in Long Beach, CA and New York City, spanning NYU and the Flatiron Institute, composed of rocket scientists, machine learning researchers, engineers, and other domain scientists. This collaborative environment at Relativity and Polymathic AI offers a unique opportunity to work on cutting edge AI models and advance AI for planetary discovery. Engineers and technicians work side by side, with deep collaboration and real-time feedback, to shape how we build better and faster. With a manifest and a launch date, it’s up to the team to deliver on Terran R: solving challenges in real time, optimizing for scale, and constantly improving processes. About the Role: Own hardware from design release through build, test, and delivery for vehicle sub-systems, taking full responsibility for execution readiness and product quality across high-volume subassemblies. or integration environment Skilled at investigating hardware issues, resolving non-conformances, and driving root cause analysis with corrective actions implemented effectively Familiar with general assembly and test procedures, including tolerance stack-up analysis, structural proof testing, and pressurized leak checks Comfortable interfacing across design, manufacturing, supply chain, and test Team members are hands-on with large-scale, complex systems including fully integrated engines and stage assemblies, pushing hardware to the limits and directly contributing to flight readiness. The work is fast-paced and highly operational, ideal for those with backgrounds in aviation, automotive, manufacturing, offshore operations, industrial systems, construction, or adjacent industries. You’ll work in a close-knit, dynamic environment where collaboration between technicians, operators, and engineers is not only encouraged, but expected. As the company scales, the Stennis Test team becomes even more critical to unlocking our next phase of growth: proving out full-stage systems and paving the way for routine, reliable flights of Terran R. About the Role: As a Propulsion Test Technician III , you will perform complex installation, maintenance, troubleshooting, and repair activities supporting propulsion test operations. This role coordinates technical work, resolves complex equipment issues, and provides operational guidance during test execution. Responsibilities Perform complex installation, maintenance, troubleshooting, and repair of propulsion test systems and facility equipment. Diagnose and resolve system-level mechanical, fluid, and instrumentation issues. Coordinate assigned technical activities supporting propulsion test operations. Fabricate and install mechanical and instrumentation systems for new or modified test facilities. Perform maintenance and functional verification of instrumentation and control components. Recommend improvements to maintenance procedures, work instructions, and equipment reliability. Support commissioning activities for new or modified test systems. Provide technical guidance to technicians during routine testing and maintenance activities. Coordinate maintenance activities to support test schedules. Perform other duties as assigned. Physical Requirements Lift a minimum of 50 lbs. unassisted. Stand for extended periods. Stoop, bend, crawl, and work in confined spaces. Work occasional night shifts and travel as required. About You: Experience supporting propulsion testing, industrial maintenance, instrumentation, controls, mechanical systems, or related technical environments. Ability to: Perform complex troubleshooting across multiple test system disciplines. Coordinate technical work activities. Interpret engineering documentation and apply it to field activities. Provide technical guidance during maintenance and testing. Identify opportunities to improve equipment reliability and work processes. Mechanical Focus Experience troubleshooting complex fluid systems, valves, regulators, and mechanical assemblies. Instrumentation Focus Experience troubleshooting instrumentation, data acquisition systems, sensors, and control hardware. Nice to haves but not required: Experience supporting commissioning of new test facilities. Experience performing root cause investigations. Successful candidates must clear a background check administered by the US government to obtain clearance for on-site work at our government partner location in Stennis, Mississippi. title: Vehicle Structures Engineer I - 2026 Graduate
description: Organisation: Relativity. Location: Long Beach, California, United States. Department: Stage Structures and Mechanisms Engineering. Office: LB - Wormhole HQ (CA). At Relativity Space, we’re building rockets to serve today’s needs and tomorrow’s breakthroughs. About the Team: The Structures and Mechanisms team is responsible for the full design, build, and test lifecycle of Terran R’s integrated structures and flight mechanisms. Whether you're working on highly iterative mechanisms that move or tight-margin structures that shouldn’t, you’ll get hands-on hardware ownership and see the rocket coming to life on the factory floor. Both teams fall under one department, sharing design principles, tools, and an integrated approach that provides a comprehensive view of Terran R. Team members work on multiple parts, not just within a single subsystem, and are empowered to make decisions that directly impact flight hardware. Beyond first flight, you’ll play a critical role in refining for manufacturability and speed. About the Role: The scope of work encompasses a full design cycle, including conceptualization, design, analysis, manufacturing and testing for primary and secondary structures related to Thrust Structure, Propellant Tanks, Interstage or Fairing, to name a few. You will need to think creatively and leverage innovation to reduce mass, parts, processes and tooling required. Your responsibilities will include, but not be limited to the following: Innovative conceptualization of structural load path, design for complex structures and adjacent system packaging. Review of static & dynamic load inputs, material properties & test as well as structural systems & subsystems requirements. Analysis and sizing of flight structures to ensure timely design reviews and drawing release. Develop and support hardware test campaigns, including test integration, operation and result evaluation. Support manufacturing process development. In order to be successful in this role, you must be someone who is self-motivated, adaptable and is able to lead your own projects to completion in a fast-paced environment. Ideally, you have significant mechanical or structural design experience and a proven track record completing collaborative projects effectively. On a weekly basis, you will be designing flight components for our upcoming Terran R vehicle using NX/TeamCenter, performing analysis using Nastran, ANSYS and/or hand calculations, creating and releasing drawings as well as supporting fabrication of your components. You will own your design from requirements to production. You will also use your strong organizational skills to properly document your work and present your recommendations when decisions are needed. About You: 0-2+ years of experience in a design engineering role. Bachelor’s degree in a related discipline. Experience with industry-standard CAD packages such as NX, Creo, or Solidworks Working knowledge of structural analysis (hand calculation, Finite Elements Methods and industry tools) and test Fundamental knowledge of structures strength, stability and fatigue failure mechanisms. Fundamental knowledge of additive and traditional manufacturing processes Full life cycle project ownership experience Hiring Timeline: We are actively hiring for immediate openings. Candidates should have completed their degree requirements and be available to begin full-time employment within 30–60 days of applying . If your availability falls outside this window, we encourage you to return and apply when you are within 30–60 days of being available to start full-time employment. Nice to haves but not required: Extensive experience with NX/TeamCenter. Expertise using Nastran and ANSYS. Experience with GD&T and drafting. title: Feature: Multi-hop document-RAG for cross-document questions
description:
Open-source contribution opportunity. Repository: trustgraph-ai/trustgraph. Labels: enhancement, help wanted, size: large. ## Summary

Document-RAG currently performs a single retrieval pass: extract concepts → embed → fetch matching chunks → synthesise answer.  This works well when the answer lives in one or two chunks, but falls short for questions that span multiple documents or require connecting information across sections.

A multi-hop retrieval loop would let the LLM read initial chunks, identify what information is still missing, and issue follow-up queries — iterating until it has enough context to answer.

## Motivation

Example questions that need multi-hop:

- *"How does the data retention policy interact with the GDPR compliance requirements?"* — retention policy is in one document, GDPR requirements in another
- *"Compare the authentication mechanisms described in the v2 and v3 architecture documents"* — needs chunks from two different documents
- *"What are all the prerequisites for deploying the production pipeline?"* — prerequisites may be scattered across setup guide, infrastructure doc, and runbook

Today these queries retrieve chunks biased toward one aspect of the question and miss the rest.

## Proposed design

Please PR against the latest `release/vX.Y` branch.

### Iterative retrieval loop

```
1. Extract concepts from query (existing step)
2. Retrieve initial chunks (existing step)
3. Loop (max N iterations):
   a. Present query + retrieved chunks to LLM with a "reflection" prompt
   b. LLM outputs either:
      - SUFFICIENT: enough context to answer → break
      - FOLLOW_UP: one or more follow-up queries for missing info
   c. For each follow-up query: extract concepts → embed → retrieve chunks
   d. Deduplicate and append to chunk set
4. Synthesise answer from full chunk set (existing step)
```

### Where it fits in the codebase

This would be a new retrieval module alongside the existing ones:

```
trustgraph-flow/trustgraph/retrieval/
├── document_rag/          # existing single-hop
│   ├── document_rag.py
│   └── rag.py
├── graph_rag/             # existing graph-based
│   ├── graph_rag.py
│   └── rag.py
└── multihop_rag/          # new
    ├── multihop_rag.py    # MultiHopRag class with iterative loop
    └── rag.py             # Processor wiring
```

The `MultiHopRag` class would reuse the existing `Query` helper from `document_rag.py` for the retrieval steps (concept extraction, embedding, chunk fetching).  The new part is the reflection/follow-up loop.

### New prompt template

A `multihop-reflection` prompt that takes:
- `query`: the original question
- `documents`: chunks retrieved so far
- Output: JSON with `status` ("sufficient" or "follow_up") and optional `follow_up_queries` list

### Configuration

- `--max-hops`: maximum retrieval iterations (default 3)
- `--doc-limit-per-hop`: chunks to fetch per follow-up query (default 5)
- `--total-doc-limit`: overall cap on accumulated chunks (default 30)

### Explainability

Each hop would emit its own exploration provenance event, so the explainability trace shows the full retrieval chain: question → hop 1 (N chunks) → hop 2 (M chunks) → synthesis.

## What you'll learn

- How TrustGraph's document-RAG and prompt systems work
- How to create a new retrieval module and wire it into the processor framework
- How to add prompt templates to the config system
- How the explainability/provenance system tracks retrieval steps

## References

- Single-hop retrieval: `trustgraph-flow/trustgraph/retrieval/document_rag/document_rag.py`
- Processor wiring: `trustgraph-flow/trustgraph/retrieval/document_rag/rag.py`
- Prompt client interface: `trustgraph-base/trustgraph/base/prompt_client.py`
- Provenance helpers: `trustgraph-flow/trustgraph/provenance/`

Engineers are responsible for the entire lifecycle of their parts, from initial design through production to qualification and flight. The team fosters a culture of bottoms-up decision-making, free from technical gatekeeping, where ownership and accountability are key at all levels. But designing engines with a quarter million pounds of thrust is just the beginning. About the Role: The COPV team is responsible for delivering the critical high-pressure gas storage vessels for Terran R. These are not simple off-the-shelf components. The team works closely with partners across the company and throughout the supply chain to ensure performance can be achieved safely, reliably, and at scale. COPVs are notoriously difficult engineering problems, with design, manufacturing, and operational challenges that span multiple disciplines and require deep technical rigor and careful execution. The product itself is deeply integrated with the rest of the vehicle, and the team maintains full ownership across design, production, test, and flight. You won’t simply execute predefined requirements; you’ll be expected to ask the right questions, collaborate across disciplines, and drive toward the best overall solution for Terran R. You will be a part of developing the architecture for the Terran R vehicle and will be responsible for charting the company’s path for gas storage on a reusable rocket- both near-term and long-term. title: test: add tests for gdpr_compliance.rego (GDPR)
description:
Open-source contribution opportunity. Repository: ynotbhatc/rego_policy_libraries. Labels: help wanted, good first issue. **File:** `frameworks/privacy/gdpr/gdpr_compliance.rego` (292 lines)
**Package:** `gdpr.compliance`
**Standard:** GDPR

This policy uses **boolean rules**: `default <name> := false` with a matching
`<name> if { ... }`. There are roughly **21** of them.

For each, write a case with input that makes it true, and one where it stays
false. Boolean rules are where the `{}` trap bites — a rule with no `default`
is *undefined* rather than false, and one undefined field collapses the whole
report object.

### Done when

- [ ] `opa test frameworks/privacy/gdpr -v` passes
- [ ] Each rule has a case that exercises it
- [ ] At least one case asserts nothing fires on compliant input
- [ ] The compliance report is asserted to be a **populated object on empty input**, not `{}`

### Where to put it

`frameworks/privacy/gdpr/tests/test_gdpr_compliance.rego`, package `gdpr.compliance_test`.

The pattern to copy, and the `array.concat` trap, are in
[CONTRIBUTING.md](../blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md). The full queue of untested
policies is in [COVERAGE.md](../blob/main/COVERAGE.md).

---

*Comment before you start so two people don't write the same test.*

title: soup loop canary writes three fields to loop.yaml and nothing reads them: no traffic split, no canary verdict, no rollback — and the pre-wired deploy records verdict "OK" on a 200
description:
Open-source contribution opportunity. Repository: MakazhanAlpamys/Soup. Labels: bug, help wanted. ## The defect

`docs/commands.md:148` advertises `soup loop canary <adapter> --traffic 5%` as "Promote canary + auto-rollback on MAJOR", and `docs/adapters-and-governance.md:123-124,133` describes a deterministic router that is "sticky-on-rollback — a flaky verdict can't ping-pong traffic between adapters". The router, the verdict and the rollback all exist as functions. None of them is called.

## Evidence

**The functions, and their callers in `src/`:**

| function | defined | callers outside its own module |
|---|---|---|
| `canary_router.route` (the traffic split) | `utils/canary_router.py:83` | none |
| `loop_daemon.evaluate_canary_verdict` | `utils/loop_daemon.py:380` | none |
| `loop_daemon.maybe_rollback` | `utils/loop_daemon.py:391` | none |
| canary `BucketStats(...)` (the per-bucket stats the verdict needs) | `utils/canary_router.py` | never constructed (the only `BucketStats(` in `src/` is an unrelated class in `utils/curriculum_dynamic.py:163`) |

They are exercised only by `tests/test_v0580.py`.

**What the command does.** `commands/loop.py:276-316` builds a `CanaryPolicy` for validation, then writes `canary_active`, `canary_traffic_pct` and `canary_autoroll_on_regress` into `.soup/loop.yaml`. The only reader of those fields is `soup loop status`, which prints them (`commands/loop.py:140-144`). Note also that `--autoroll-on-regress` is passed into the policy as `sticky_on_rollback` (line 298), a different property.

**What the pre-wired deploy stage does.** `utils/loop_stages.py:370-376`:

```python
ok = _post_activate(endpoint, name)
return {"deployed": ok, "canary_verdict": "OK" if ok else None, ...}
```

The verdict is "OK" whenever the activate POST returns 2xx. And the endpoint it calls, `POST /v1/adapters/activate/{name}` (`commands/serve.py:1797-1811`), sets a single process-global `active_state["active"] = name` — it switches **all** traffic to the new adapter. So the pre-wired loop's "canary" is a 100% cutover whose verdict is decided before any request has been served on it.

#176 (closed) wired the harvest / train / gate / deploy stage callbacks; it did not cover routing, verdict or rollback, and they have stayed unwired since v0.58.0.

## Reproduction

```
$ soup loop init stable-adapter --eval evals/lock.json --baseline prod
$ soup loop canary candidate-adapter --traffic 5% --autoroll-on-regress
canary set: candidate-adapter @ 5.0% (autoroll=True)
exit=0
$ soup loop status
│ canary           │ candidate-adapter @ 5.0% │
$ cat .soup/loop.yaml
  "canary_active": "candidate-adapter",
  "canary_autoroll_on_regress": true,
  "canary_traffic_pct": 5.0,
```

That is the entire effect. Nothing in `soup serve` or `soup loop watch` reads the three fields.

The pre-wired deploy stage, called directly against a local HTTP server that answers every POST with 200:

```
server received: ['/v1/adapters/activate/adapter']
deploy_to_canary returned: {'deployed': True, 'canary_verdict': 'OK', 'notes': ''}
```

Grep to confirm the missing callers:

```bash
grep -rn "\.route(\|maybe_rollback\|evaluate_canary_verdict\|canary_traffic_pct" src/soup_cli --include=*.py
```

## Why it matters

A canary is a gate: its entire purpose is to expose a new adapter to a small share of traffic, measure it, and pull it back if it regresses. An operator who runs `soup loop canary ... --traffic 5% --autoroll-on-regress` believes 95% of traffic is protected and that a MAJOR regression reverts automatically. In fact no traffic moves at all via this command, and in the pre-wired loop 100% moves with a recorded "OK" verdict and no mechanism that could ever record MAJOR. The iteration manifest (`loop_iteration.py:43`) then carries that "OK" as evidence.

## Proposed fix

Either wire it or stop advertising it; both are acceptable, the current middle state is not.

**Wire it:**
1. `soup serve` reads the canary policy (from `loop.yaml` or a flag) and calls `canary_router.route(policy, conversation_id)` per request, so the configured percentage is real. `/v1/adapters/activate` stays a cutover and is not what the loop's deploy stage calls.
2. Record per-bucket outcomes (judge score, refusal, error rate — whatever the eval suite measures) into `BucketStats`, and have `soup loop watch` periodically call `evaluate_canary_verdict` and `maybe_rollback` when `canary_autoroll_on_regress` is set, persisting the rolled-back policy.
3. The deploy stage records `canary_verdict: None` (or `"UNKNOWN"`) at promotion time; a verdict is only written once there is data behind it.
4. Keep `sticky_on_rollback` and "autoroll on regress" as separate options.

**Or, until then:** mark `soup loop canary` as recording intent only, print that in its output, change the docs, and have the deploy stage record `UNKNOWN` instead of `OK`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A test that promotes a canary at 5% and sends N requests with distinct conversation ids through the serve app asserts that roughly 5% (not 0%, not 100%) are served by the canary adapter. It FAILS on current code.
- [ ] A test that feeds MAJOR-level bucket stats to the running loop asserts `loop.yaml` ends with the canary cleared. It FAILS on current code.
- [ ] `deploy_to_canary` no longer returns `canary_verdict: "OK"` from a successful POST alone; a test pins this.
- [ ] `docs/commands.md` and `docs/adapters-and-governance.md` describe what actually happens.

Although this behavior disappeared in v2.0.7 (together with the ability to set a separate naming model), this raise the concern that Cherry Studio will upload my conversation history to its official provider for processing by default in some versions, separate from the data collection switch provided in the settings, which is potentially against the [privacy policy](https://docs.cherryai.com.cn/about/privacypolicy), which states that: "We explicitly commit not to collect, store, transmit, or process the following data:... your conversation data". Further research point out that the model is provided by SiliconFlow, according to [this official documentation](https://docs.cherryai.com.cn/pre-basic/providers/cherryai/free-qwen.md). In other words, Cherry Studio has connected users to a third-party provider **by default** without the consent and acknowledgement from users. Even if this is not the default behavior, the current model description read "Provider: CherryAI", and does not allow the user to modify, delete such provider. This contradicts with the description of the privacy policy: "Since this software utilizes an API key from a third-party model service provider—which you obtain and configure yourself—you are effectively receiving services directly from that provider when using the AI ​​chat function." Categorically, the user did not obtain and configure any third-party model, yet is still connected to a third-party provider. Furthermore, because of the description of how the free provider operates directly states that ["Cherry server"](https://docs.cherryai.com.cn/pre-basic/providers/cherryai.md) is involved in the operation, we have a reasonable suspicion that Cherry is involved with the transmit and process of our conversation data, which potentially contradict with your privacy policy. We would like the following disclosure and changes to be made: 1. Explicitly list the third-party providers Cherry utilizes for build-in provider in the model description, change the privacy policy to acknowledge such facts, and ask for explicit consent before user send its first message to such providers. 2. An explicit, written statement in policy or docs that disclose how Cherry handles data for the build-in provider, include but not limited to: the data collected, telemetry data send to third party provider, whether prompts/responses pass through Cherry servers, retention/logging practice, etc. 3. Add the ability for users to explicitly turn off the build-in provider. ### Context _No response_ ### Additional Information ```shell ``` ### Priority Low (Review when available)

title: [Ethics] Research-ethics review (IRB equivalent) for real-household pilots
description:
Open-source contribution opportunity. Repository: lumenaut-llc/oesis-program-specs. Labels: help wanted, phase: v1.0, node: platform, area: governance, severity: important, program: ethics-equity. ## Summary

Pilots with real households participating in smoke/heat/flood hazard monitoring are research on human subjects, even if informal. Requires a review process analogous to IRB: informed consent beyond product consent, vulnerability assessment, risk-benefit analysis, withdrawal protection.

## Why this matters

Tier B external pilots will use real participant data. Consent checklists (PI-1) and participant notices (PI-4) handle product consent. **Research ethics is distinct** — it's about the pilot *as research*, whether academic or not. CITI/IRB norms apply even to informal civic-tech research.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Review process at `legal/research-ethics-review.md` (new).
- [ ] Pre-pilot review template (risk, benefit, consent, vulnerability, withdrawal, data handling).
- [ ] Reviewer roles (can be internal for early pilots; must escalate if any red flag).
- [ ] Cross-reference UA5 pilot governance framework and PI-1/PI-4 consent + notice.
- [ ] Escalation to external IRB criteria (federally-funded work, vulnerable populations, etc.).

## How to start

1. Read CITI IRB basics + civic-tech research-ethics writings (e.g., Data & Society).
2. Draft review template.
3. Draft escalation criteria.
4. Legal review.
5. PR.
